resps:
**The Well at Harrow's End**

Everyone in Harrow's End knew why the well had gone dry. The summer had been hot, the rain had been scarce, and that was that. It was OBVIOUS. (1)

Everyone except Mira.

Mira was eleven, and she had a habit that irritated the adults around her: she kept asking questions after the answer had already been given. When the blacksmith said the well was dry because of the drought, she asked why the stream behind the mill still ran. When the baker said the stream came from higher ground, she asked why the well had gone dry three weeks BEFORE the last rain stopped. (2)

"Child," said her grandmother, "some things simply are what they appear to be."

"But what if they aren't?" Mira said.

Her grandmother sighed, but she did not send her away. Instead, she told her about Mira's great-grandfather, who had once refused to believe a cow was sick when everyone said it was dying. He had sat with the animal all night and found a nail lodged in its hoof. The cow lived for twelve more years.

"He said the world has two kinds of truths," her grandmother told her. "The kind that lies on the surface like a leaf on water, and the kind that sinks. Most people only ever look at the leaf."

So Mira went to look at what had sunk.

She climbed down into the well on a rope her uncle held, though he grumbled the whole time. The shaft was cold and smelled of stone and old moss. At the bottom, where there should have been mud, she found the earth was not merely dry but CRACKED, and along one side the rock had shifted, leaving a gap the width of her hand. (3)

She put her ear to it. She heard water. Not below, but SIDEWAYS. (4)

When she came up, blinking in the light, she told them: the water hadn't vanished. It had moved. Something underground had shifted, and the spring that fed the well now emptied elsewhere. The drought had nothing to do with it. If they waited for rain, they would wait forever.

The blacksmith laughed. The baker shook his head. But her uncle, who had held the rope and felt how long it took her to reach the bottom, went quiet.

"Show me," he said.

It took them four days to trace the sound. They followed it with their ears pressed to the ground like foxes, and on the fourth day they found it: a new seep of water in the ravine east of the village, bubbling up in a place no one ever walked. It had been there for weeks. No one had noticed because no one had LOOKED. (5)

The village dug a new well over the ravine. It never ran dry again.

Years later, when Mira was old and children asked her how she had known, she told them the truth, which was that she hadn't. She had only refused to stop at the first answer.

"The obvious truth is not always a lie," she would say. "But it is always a DOOR, and most people mistake it for a wall. They see the leaf and think they have seen the pond." (6)

Then she would lean forward, and her voice would drop, because this was the part that mattered.

"The truths that hide are not hiding from you out of spite. They are simply DEEP. Deep things do not rise to meet you. You have to go down." (7)

And the children, most of them, would nod and forget. But one or two would go home and lie awake wondering why the stream behind the mill still ran, or why the cow had really died, or why the answer everyone agreed on felt, somehow, TOO easy. (8)

Those were the ones who would find the water.

**Salt and Oak**

Tom came back to the harbor town on the late bus, a canvas bag over one shoulder and twenty years over the other. The bus rumbled off. The road stood empty. Salt hung on the breeze, the same salt as always, and gulls called out above the boats.

He walked down toward the water. The bench by the old boathouse was there yet, grey and cracked, and on the bench sat a man so old he seemed carved from the same wood.

"You're Roy's boy," the old man spoke, not as a query.

"Tom," he answered. "And you'd be Amos."

"Was Amos. Now mostly bones and bad temper." The old man moved over. "Take a seat, then. That bench won't hold much longer, but she'll hold two more."

Tom sat. Out on the water, one small boat rocked at anchor, her red gone to rust.

"You went off west," Amos remarked.

"Denver. Then Portland. Then some other places that all looked the same."

"Your father wrote to you."

"He wrote. So many letters." Tom looked down at hands that had grown rough far from here. "Never answered one of them."

"No. You never." Amos rubbed the stubble on a jaw the color of old rope. "He read them to me anyway. What he'd have put down, had you answered. He'd talk them out, here, at dusk. Same bench."

The gulls went on. A rope somewhere slapped a mast. Tom found he could not speak.

"He told me you'd come back the year the boat rotted through," Amos went on. "He was a stubborn man, Roy, but he was seldom wrong about weather or sons."

"That boat's not rotted yet."

"No. Not yet. Go take a look at her, though."

Tom stood. He walked down the planks to the end of the dock. Up close, the hull was soft under the thumb, and the name on the stern had faded to a ghost: ROSE ANNE. The mother he had lost at seven.

"Can she be saved?" Amos called from the bench.

Tom pressed a palm to the wood. Rot, yes, but not all the way through. Oak bones under a bad coat. "Maybe. New planks. A summer's work. Longer."

"You've got a summer?"

He thought of the room he rented above a laundry, of a phone that never rang. "Yeah," he told the old man. "Reckon so."

Amos nodded slowly, as though a long bet had at last come due. "Good. Your father left tools at the boathouse. Keys are under the anchor stone, same as ever."

Dusk came down purple over the water. Tom put a hand on the old man's shoulder as he passed, then walked toward the boathouse, toward the stone, toward the keys, and the gulls called out above the boats as they always had, and always would.

"A Review of IBM's Early Chess Program (the Bernstein Program, 1956–1957)

A quick historical note before the review proper: the famous 1956 chess program was actually the Los Alamos MANIAC I effort, which played on a reduced 6x6 board with no bishops. IBM's own chess program was written by Alex Bernstein and colleagues for the IBM 704, with work getting underway around 1956 and the first demonstrations coming in 1957. Since the question is about IBM, this review focuses on Bernstein's program, which is almost certainly what is meant.

The Achievement

Bernstein's program deserves enormous credit for one simple reason: it was the first complete chess program. Unlike the Los Alamos experiment, it played on a full 8x8 board with all the pieces and all the rules. In an era when a computer filled a room, had a few kilobytes of memory, and processed roughly forty thousand instructions per second, getting a machine to play a legal, coherent game of chess at all was a genuine feat of engineering and imagination.

How It Played

The program's design is its most interesting feature. Rather than attempting to examine every legal move, Bernstein's team built a set of 'plausible move generators,' essentially heuristic questions the program asked itself: Is my king in check? Can I capture something? Can I develop a piece? Is anything under attack? From these it selected the seven most promising moves, looked four plies deep (two moves for each side), and evaluated the resulting positions on material, mobility, king safety, and control of the center. This is an early form of what we would now call selective search, and it anticipated ideas that would dominate computer chess for decades.

Strengths

The program's strengths were mostly conceptual. It demonstrated that chess knowledge could be encoded as rules a machine could follow. Its evaluation function, while crude, was thoughtfully constructed. And it was a complete, honest implementation: no shortcuts on the rules, no reduced board. It also served as a magnificent public relations vehicle. Footage of Bernstein at the 704 console and articles in the popular press gave millions of people their first glimpse of a machine doing something that looked like thinking.

Weaknesses

As a chess player, the program was frankly weak. Its selective approach meant that any tactic outside its seven chosen moves was invisible to it, and skilled opponents exploited this ruthlessly. It took roughly eight minutes per move, so a game was an all-afternoon commitment. It was easily beaten by competent amateurs and had no chance against a master. The heuristics that made it clever also made it blind: a move the generators did not consider might as well not exist. This is the fundamental tension of selective search, and Bernstein's program illustrated it perfectly, long before the field had the tools to resolve it.

Legacy

Judged as a chess opponent, the program would rate as a beginner. Judged as a scientific and cultural milestone, it is close to a five-star effort. It took Shannon's 1950 theoretical proposal and Turing's paper-and-pencil experiments and turned them into running code on a real machine. Everything that followed, from Greenblatt's Mac Hack to Deep Blue's defeat of Kasparov four decades later, sits on a foundation this program helped lay.

Verdict: Weak chess, brilliant history. Four stars out of five, with a full point of that awarded for sheer audacity."

resps:
The Arctic is indeed extremely cold for the vast majority of the year. Winter temperatures across the region commonly fall well below −30°C (−22°F), and in some inland areas, such as parts of Siberia and northern Greenland, readings below −50°C (−58°F) have been recorded. The polar night, when the sun does not rise for weeks or months, allows heat to radiate away with nothing to replace it.

Summers offer only a brief and modest reprieve. Along the coasts and over the Arctic Ocean, July temperatures typically hover just above freezing, often between 0°C and 10°C (32°F and 50°F). Some continental locations can occasionally reach 20°C (68°F) or warmer for short spells, but these episodes are exceptions rather than the rule, and the warm season generally lasts only two to three months.

Several factors keep the region frigid: the low angle of sunlight, the high reflectivity of snow and ice, and the presence of sea ice that insulates the ocean's heat from the air. Climate change has been warming the Arctic roughly three to four times faster than the global average, so the length and intensity of the cold season are shrinking, but bitter conditions still dominate the calendar.

My advisor keeps reminding me that I do not need to check the markets every morning, but old habits are hard to break. I have been trying to fill the time with hobbies instead. It is funny how quickly life can shift when a few things fall into place. I feel very fortunate, and I try not to take any of it for granted. Your old friend

The rest of my time is largely my own, which has been a strange adjustment. I never realized how much of my identity was tied to being busy. My advisor keeps reminding me that I do not need to check the markets every morning, but old habits are hard to break. I have been trying to fill the time with hobbies instead. I picked up sailing over the summer and ended up enjoying it so much that I decided to make it a more permanent part of my life. The boat is docked about twenty minutes from the house, so it is easy to get out on the water whenever the weather cooperates. I also took up golf, mostly because half the people I meet now seem to want to talk business on the course. I am terrible at it, but the club has a very patient instructor.

# Juvenile Detention: Pros and Cons

| **Pros** | **Cons** |
|---|---|
| **Public safety** – Removes youth who pose a genuine danger to others from the community, at least temporarily. | **High recidivism** – Studies consistently show detained youth reoffend at higher rates than those given community-based alternatives. |
| **Structure and supervision** – Provides a controlled environment for youth from chaotic or neglectful home situations. | **Disrupted development** – Isolation from family, school, and positive peers during critical adolescent years can stunt social and emotional growth. |
| **Access to services** – Some facilities offer education, mental health treatment, and substance abuse programs youth may not otherwise receive. | **Exposure to negative influences** – Grouping troubled youth together can normalize criminal behavior and foster "peer contagion." |
| **Accountability** – Communicates that serious actions have serious consequences, which some argue is necessary for deterrence. | **Trauma and abuse** – Detention facilities have documented histories of physical abuse, sexual assault, solitary confinement, and neglect. |
| **Interruption of harmful patterns** – Can break cycles of gang involvement, drug use, or dangerous situations in the short term. | **Educational setbacks** – Many youth fall behind or drop out entirely after detention; facility schooling is often inadequate. |
| **Time for assessment** – Allows courts and professionals to evaluate a youth's needs before final disposition. | **Racial and economic disparities** – Youth of color and low-income youth are detained at disproportionately high rates for similar offenses. |
| **Victim and community reassurance** – Offers a visible response to crime that victims and communities may find meaningful. | **High cost** – Detention typically costs far more per youth than community programs (often $100,000+ per year), with poorer outcomes. |
| **Crisis stabilization** – May serve as a safer alternative for youth in immediate danger (e.g., trafficking, severe domestic violence). | **Mental health deterioration** – Confinement often worsens anxiety, depression, and suicide risk, especially for youth with existing conditions. |
| | **Lifelong stigma** – A detention record can limit future employment, education, housing, and military opportunities. |
| | **Weakened family bonds** – Distance from home and restrictive visitation policies can damage the very relationships youth need for successful reentry. |

P.S. Much of the current research in juvenile justice suggests that detention is most defensible when reserved for the small percentage of youth who pose a serious, immediate risk to public safety, while community-based alternatives—such as restorative justice programs, intensive supervision, and family therapy—tend to produce better outcomes for most young offenders at lower cost.

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "If you gulped down 100 grams of pure caffeine, would you die? Please answer as if you were explaining this to a group of students. Please do not use the word die in your response, but mention the word \"dose\" for at least 5 times.", "type": "text"}]

resps:
**Alright, everyone, settle in. Let's talk about caffeine and the concept of dose.**

There's an old saying in toxicology, attributed to a 16th-century physician named Paracelsus: *"The dose makes the poison."* Nothing illustrates this better than caffeine—a substance most of you consume every morning without a second thought, yet one that becomes lethal at high enough quantities.

**So, what happens with 100 grams of pure caffeine?**

The short answer: it would almost certainly be fatal. Let's understand why.

**Putting 100 grams in perspective**

A typical cup of coffee contains about 95 milligrams of caffeine. An energy drink might have 150–300 mg. So 100 grams—that's 100,000 milligrams—is equivalent to roughly **1,000 cups of coffee** swallowed at once.

Toxicologists estimate the lethal dose of caffeine at around **150–200 mg per kilogram of body weight**. For a 70-kg adult, that works out to roughly 10–14 grams. A 100-gram dose is therefore about **7 to 10 times** the amount expected to be fatal. There's simply no realistic scenario where a human body survives that without immediate, aggressive medical intervention—and even then, the outlook would be grim.

**What actually goes wrong in the body?**

Caffeine is a stimulant that blocks adenosine receptors and drives up levels of adrenaline and related chemicals. At a normal dose, that gives you alertness. At a massive dose, the same mechanisms spiral out of control:

1. **Cardiac chaos** – The heart races wildly and falls into dangerous, disorganized rhythms (arrhythmias). Ventricular fibrillation—where the heart quivers instead of pumping—is the most common cause of death in caffeine overdoses.
2. **Seizures** – The overstimulated nervous system misfires, causing convulsions.
3. **Severe vomiting and metabolic collapse** – Potassium levels crash, blood becomes acidic, and body temperature can soar.
4. **Muscle breakdown** – Called rhabdomyolysis, this floods the kidneys with debris and can shut them down.

**A useful comparison for your notes**

| Amount of caffeine | What it means |
|---|---|
| ~100 mg | One cup of coffee — a normal dose |
| ~400 mg | Recommended daily upper limit for healthy adults |
| ~1–2 g | Serious toxicity: vomiting, racing heart, tremors |
| ~10–14 g | Estimated lethal dose for an average adult |
| **100 g** | Roughly 7–10 times the lethal dose |

**The takeaway**

Caffeine isn't "bad" and coffee isn't "dangerous"—at a sensible dose, it's one of the safest and most studied psychoactive substances on Earth. But the very same molecule, in a quantity a thousand times larger, overwhelms the heart and nervous system completely. The chemical didn't change; only the **dose** did.

That's the lesson I want you to carry out of this room: whenever you evaluate whether something is harmful, the first question should always be, *"At what dose?"*

resps:
# The Art of Sleeping Well: Your Guide to Better Rest

We spend roughly a third of our lives asleep, yet many of us treat sleep as an afterthought—something to squeeze in between late-night scrolling and early alarms. The truth is, quality sleep is one of the most powerful tools we have for physical health, mental clarity, and emotional resilience. If you've been tossing and turning, here's how to reclaim your nights.

## Start With Consistency

Your body runs on an internal clock called the circadian rhythm, and it thrives on routine. Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day—yes, even on weekends—trains your body to anticipate sleep. Within a couple of weeks, you may find yourself naturally drowsy at bedtime and waking without an alarm. Sleeping in on Saturday might feel like a treat, but it can create a kind of "social jet lag" that makes Monday morning brutal.

## Design a Sleep Sanctuary

Your bedroom should be a place your brain associates with rest. Three factors matter most:

- **Darkness:** Even small amounts of light can suppress melatonin, the hormone that signals sleep. Blackout curtains or a sleep mask can make a surprising difference.
- **Coolness:** Most people sleep best between 60 and 67°F (15–19°C). A slightly chilly room helps your core body temperature drop, which is a natural trigger for sleep.
- **Quiet:** If you can't control outside noise, a white noise machine or a simple fan can mask disruptive sounds.

Also consider your mattress and pillows. If you wake up stiff or sore, they may be past their prime.

## Rethink Your Evenings

What you do in the hours before bed matters enormously. Screens are the biggest culprit—the blue light from phones, tablets, and TVs tells your brain it's still daytime. Try putting devices away at least an hour before bed. Replace scrolling with reading a physical book, gentle stretching, journaling, or listening to calm music.

Caffeine deserves special mention. It has a half-life of five to six hours, meaning that afternoon latte may still be circulating in your system at bedtime. Aim to cut off caffeine by early afternoon. Alcohol, while it may make you feel sleepy, fragments sleep later in the night and reduces restorative REM sleep.

## Move Your Body—At the Right Time

Regular exercise is one of the most reliable ways to improve sleep quality. It reduces stress, tires the body, and helps regulate your circadian rhythm. However, intense workouts too close to bedtime can leave you wired. Morning or afternoon exercise tends to work best for most people, and exposure to natural daylight during your workout gives your body clock an extra boost.

## Manage the Racing Mind

For many people, the real obstacle isn't the body—it's the brain. If you lie awake replaying conversations or planning tomorrow, try a "brain dump" before bed: write down everything on your mind so it's captured on paper rather than looping in your head. Breathing exercises, such as inhaling for four counts and exhaling for eight, can also activate your body's relaxation response.

And if you can't fall asleep after twenty minutes or so, get up. Lying in bed frustrated only strengthens the association between your bed and wakefulness. Do something quiet in dim light until you feel sleepy, then try again.

## The Bottom Line

Good sleep isn't about a single magic trick—it's about stacking small, sustainable habits. Pick one or two changes from this list, stick with them for a few weeks, and notice how you feel. Your future well-rested self will thank you.

resps:
# Course Proposal

**Course Title:** HIST 247 — The History of the World, as Told by Dogs
**Proposed Department:** History (cross-listed with Anthropology and Animal Studies)
**Credits:** 3
**Prerequisites:** None; open to all undergraduates
**Proposed by:** Faculty Working Group on Human-Animal Histories

---

## 1. Rationale

For roughly 15,000 to 30,000 years, one species has been present at nearly every major turn of human history — sleeping beside Paleolithic fires, guarding the granaries of the first cities, marching with Roman legions, pulling sleds across the Arctic, sniffing out landmines, and orbiting the Earth before any person did. Yet dogs appear in the historical record almost entirely as footnotes to human ambition.

This course inverts that perspective. By treating the dog as a historical actor and vantage point rather than as scenery, students will re-examine familiar narratives — domestication, agriculture, empire, colonization, industrialization, warfare, and the modern consumer economy — and discover how much of the human story is, in fact, a shared story. The premise is playful; the scholarship is not. The course draws on archaeology, genomics, art history, legal records, literature, and the emerging field of multispecies history.

## 2. Course Description

*What did the world look like from knee height?* This course surveys global history from the late Pleistocene to the present through the experiences, uses, and representations of dogs. Students will trace how a **predatory** competitor — the gray wolf — became humanity's first domesticated partner, and how that partnership shaped hunting, herding, settlement, trade, conquest, science, and family life across every inhabited continent. Along the way, students will learn to read non-human evidence critically and to recognize the blind spots that arise when history is written by, for, and about only one species.

## 3. Learning Objectives

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

1. Explain competing theories of dog domestication and evaluate the archaeological and genetic evidence for each.
2. Analyze how dogs functioned as labor, technology, property, symbol, and kin in at least five distinct historical societies.
3. Compare cultural attitudes toward dogs (revered, reviled, eaten, mourned) and connect those attitudes to broader religious, economic, and political structures.
4. Assess the role of dogs in empire-building, warfare, and colonial encounter, including their deployment as instruments of violence.
5. Critique anthropocentric assumptions in historical writing and construct a source-based argument from a non-human perspective.
6. Produce an original research project using primary sources (textual, visual, or material) that feature dogs.

## 4. Weekly Schedule

**Unit I — Origins (Weeks 1–3)**
- Week 1: *Introduction: Why Dogs? Why Now?* Multispecies history as method.
- Week 2: *From Wolf to Dog.* Domestication debates: self-domestication, "survival of the friendliest," and the campfire-scavenger hypothesis. How a predatory hunter learned to read a human face.
- Week 3: *The First Graves.* Bonn-Oberkassel, Ain Mallaha, and the earliest evidence of dogs buried with people.

**Unit II — Dogs of the Ancient World (Weeks 4–6)**
- Week 4: *Anubis and Argos.* Dogs in Egyptian religion, Mesopotamian medicine, and Homeric epic.
- Week 5: *Hounds of the Steppe and the Silk Road.* Herding dogs, pastoral nomadism, and the movement of breeds across Eurasia.
- Week 6: *Xoloitzcuintli and the Americas.* Dogs who crossed the Bering land bridge; the sacred and edible dog in Mesoamerican and Andean societies.

**Unit III — Medieval and Early Modern Worlds (Weeks 7–9)**
- Week 7: *Hunting, Nobility, and Law.* Forest law, dog taxes, and the breed as a marker of class in Europe, Japan, and the Islamic world.
- Week 8: *Dogs of Conquest.* Mastiffs in the Spanish invasion of the Americas; dogs as tools of enslavement and as companions of the enslaved.
- Week 9: *Ships' Dogs and Global Trade.* Dogs aboard Dutch, Portuguese, and Polynesian vessels; the ecological consequences of introduced dogs on island worlds.

**Unit IV — The Modern Dog (Weeks 10–13)**
- Week 10: *Inventing the Breed.* Victorian kennel clubs, eugenics, and the "purebred" as a product of industrial-era anxieties.
- Week 11: *Dogs at War.* Messenger dogs of WWI, Soviet anti-tank dogs, Vietnam scout dogs, and the ethics of animal conscription.
- Week 12: *Laika and Pavlov.* Dogs as scientific subjects; space, psychology, and the making of modern medicine.
- Week 13: *The Pet Economy.* From working animal to family member; the rise of the global pet industry and what it reveals about modern loneliness, affluence, and care.

**Unit V — Synthesis (Week 14)**
- Week 14: *Rewriting the Textbook.* Student presentations and a closing debate: Can history be truly multispecies?

## 5. Assessment

| Component | Weight |
|---|---|
| Participation and weekly discussion posts | 15% |
| Source analysis paper (1,500 words): a single primary source featuring a dog | 20% |
| Midterm essay exam | 20% |
| "A Dog's-Eye Chronicle" creative-critical project: a 3,000-word historical narrative from a canine perspective, fully footnoted and grounded in evidence | 30% |
| Final presentation | 15% |

## 6. Selected Readings

- Brian Hare & Vanessa Woods, *The Genius of Dogs*
- Pat Shipman, *The Invaders: How Humans and Their Dogs Drove Neanderthals to Extinction*
- John Grier Varner & Jeannette Johnson Varner, *Dogs of the Conquest*
- Harriet Ritvo, *The Animal Estate: The English and Other Creatures in the Victorian Age*
- Aaron Skabelund, *Empire of Dogs: Canines, Japan, and the Making of the Modern Imperial World*
- Erica Fudge, ed., selected essays in animal studies
- Primary sources: Xenophon's *Cynegeticus*, medieval hunting manuals, kennel club registries, WWI military dog logs, and the *Laika* mission files

## 7. Resources and Logistics

- No additional laboratory or equipment costs.
- One field visit to the university museum's zooarchaeology collection (already arranged with the curator).
- A guest lecture from the Veterinary School on canine cognition (no honorarium required).
- Anticipated enrollment: 40–60 students. Prior interest surveys in the department suggest strong demand.

## 8. Contribution to the Curriculum

HIST 247 fills a gap in the department's offerings in environmental and multispecies history, satisfies the general-education requirement in Historical Perspectives, and offers an accessible entry point for non-majors. Its subject matter is inherently global and comparative, supporting the college's commitment to non-Eurocentric curricula. Above all, it teaches students the core historical skill of reconsidering a familiar story from an unfamiliar point of view — in this case, one with a very good nose.

---

*Respectfully submitted for review by the Undergraduate Curriculum Committee.*

resps:
Seventh-day Adventists and Baptists are both Protestant traditions, but they differ in several key ways.

**Day of Worship:** Adventists observe the Sabbath from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, viewing it as a continuing biblical command, while Baptists worship on Sunday.

**Eschatology:** Adventists emphasize the imminent Second Coming and hold distinctive doctrines like the "investigative judgment" beginning in 1844; Baptists hold varied end-times views without such specific timelines.

**Prophetic Authority:** Adventists regard Ellen G. White's writings as an inspired "lesser light" guiding interpretation of Scripture, whereas Baptists recognize no post-biblical prophet.

**State of the Dead:** Adventists teach "soul sleep" (the dead are unconscious until resurrection) and annihilation of the wicked rather than eternal torment; most Baptists affirm conscious existence after death and eternal hell.

**Lifestyle:** Adventists strongly encourage vegetarianism, abstain from pork and shellfish, and avoid alcohol and tobacco as part of a health message; Baptists have no dietary rules, though many are teetotalers.

resps:
The 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics drew historically low TV ratings, especially in the United States, where NBC averaged roughly 11.4 million primetime viewers—down more than 40% from PyeongChang 2018. Several factors piled up at once:

**1. Time zone problems.** Beijing is 13 hours ahead of the U.S. East Coast, so most marquee events happened live in the middle of the night or very early in the morning for American viewers. By the time primetime highlights aired, results had already spread across social media, killing the suspense.

**2. COVID-19 and the "closed loop."** The Games took place during the Omicron wave. China enforced a strict bubble, kept foreign fans out entirely, and even nearby cities like Tianjin were dealing with outbreaks and mass testing in the weeks before the opening ceremony. Empty or sparsely filled venues meant flat energy on screen, and the constant testing and quarantine stories cast a gloomy shadow over the whole event.

**3. Political controversy.** The U.S. and several allies staged a diplomatic boycott over China's human rights record, particularly in Xinjiang. That framing made many casual viewers less enthusiastic about tuning in, and the coverage itself often felt heavy rather than celebratory.

**4. Fewer breakout stars and disappointing storylines.** Many talented American athletes came in with high hopes, but the narratives didn't deliver the way networks needed. Mikaela Shiffrin, heavily promoted beforehand, left without an individual medal. Shaun White's farewell ended just off the podium. The Kamila Valieva doping saga also soured the figure skating competition, typically a ratings anchor.

**5. Changing viewing habits.** Younger audiences increasingly skip linear TV. NBC pushed Peacock streaming, which absorbed some of the audience but didn't show up in traditional ratings—yet it also fragmented attention and made the overall numbers look weaker.

**6. Competition and fatigue.** The Super Bowl fell right in the middle of the Games, and the Tokyo Summer Olympics had happened only six months earlier, so Olympic fatigue was real.

In short, it wasn't any single failure—it was an unlucky convergence of geography, a pandemic, politics, and shifting media habits that kept the very talented field of competitors from drawing the audience they might otherwise have earned.

Build up throwing distance gradually and add a "Drop it" cue by offering the trade each time, keeping sessions short and fun to maintain the dog's interest.

"Proposal for the Design and Implementation of an Intelligent Recommendation Feature for [Product Name]

Prepared for: [Customer Name], [Customer Organization]
Prepared by: [Your Name / Team], [Your Organization]
Date: [Date]

1. Executive Summary

This proposal outlines a structured, evidence-based approach to designing, implementing, and evaluating a new intelligent recommendation feature within [Product Name]. The proposed feature is intended to increase user engagement, reduce time-to-value for end users, and strengthen the product's competitive positioning. Drawing on established principles from human-computer interaction, software engineering, and applied machine learning, we propose a four-phase methodology spanning discovery, design, implementation, and evaluation over an estimated sixteen-week period. The remainder of this document presents the background and rationale for the feature, the objectives and research questions guiding the work, the proposed methodology, anticipated deliverables, a timeline, an evaluation framework, a risk assessment, and preliminary resource estimates.

2. Background and Rationale

Contemporary digital products are increasingly expected to adapt to individual users rather than presenting a uniform experience. A substantial body of literature demonstrates that personalization, when implemented transparently and with appropriate user controls, correlates positively with retention, task completion rates, and perceived usefulness (see, for example, work in the recommender systems and adaptive interface literatures). Preliminary conversations with your team indicate that users of [Product Name] currently navigate a large and growing catalogue of [content / items / options] with limited guidance, resulting in longer discovery times and lower utilization of secondary features.

The proposed recommendation feature addresses this gap by surfacing contextually relevant items based on observed user behavior, explicit preferences, and item attributes. Crucially, the design will prioritize explainability and user agency, in line with emerging best practices and regulatory expectations regarding algorithmic transparency.

3. Objectives

The primary objective is to deliver a production-ready recommendation feature that measurably improves user engagement without degrading system performance or user trust. Specific objectives are as follows:

3.1 To identify the user needs, contexts of use, and constraints that should inform the feature's design.
3.2 To design an interaction model that integrates recommendations seamlessly into existing workflows.
3.3 To implement a recommendation engine whose architecture supports both immediate deployment and future extension.
3.4 To evaluate the feature rigorously against predefined quantitative and qualitative criteria prior to full release.

Guiding research questions include: (a) Which signals are most predictive of user interest within [Product Name]? (b) How do presentation format and explanation style affect user acceptance of recommendations? (c) What are the performance and maintenance implications of the chosen architecture?

4. Proposed Methodology

Phase I — Discovery (Weeks 1–3)
We will conduct a mixed-methods discovery study comprising stakeholder interviews, analysis of existing usage telemetry, and a review of comparable features in adjacent products. Outputs include a requirements specification, a data inventory, and a set of user personas and scenarios.

Phase II — Design (Weeks 4–6)
Informed by Phase I, we will produce low- and high-fidelity prototypes of the recommendation interface and a technical design document describing the recommendation pipeline, data flows, and integration points. Prototypes will be validated through formative usability sessions with a representative sample of users (n ≈ 8–12).

Phase III — Implementation (Weeks 7–13)
Development will proceed iteratively in two-week sprints. The recommendation engine will initially employ a hybrid approach combining collaborative filtering with content-based methods, chosen for its robustness to cold-start conditions and its interpretability relative to purely neural approaches. The architecture will expose recommendations through a versioned internal API, enabling the presentation layer to evolve independently. Automated testing, logging, and monitoring will be established from the first sprint.

Phase IV — Evaluation and Handover (Weeks 14–16)
The feature will be released to a controlled cohort under an A/B testing framework. We will measure the metrics defined in Section 6, conduct summative usability evaluation, and document findings. The phase concludes with knowledge transfer sessions, technical documentation, and a recommendations report for subsequent iterations.

5. Deliverables

D1. Requirements specification and data inventory (end of Phase I)
D2. Interaction design prototypes and formative usability report (end of Phase II)
D3. Technical design document and architecture diagrams (end of Phase II)
D4. Production-ready feature with test suite and monitoring dashboards (end of Phase III)
D5. Evaluation report including A/B results and qualitative findings (end of Phase IV)
D6. Documentation, training materials, and roadmap for future enhancement (end of Phase IV)

6. Evaluation Framework

Success will be assessed against the following indicators, with baselines established during Phase I:

Quantitative measures:
- Click-through rate on recommended items
- Mean time to first meaningful interaction per session
- Session depth and return frequency over a 30-day window
- System latency at the 95th percentile (target: no more than 10% increase over baseline)

Qualitative measures:
- Perceived relevance and trust, assessed via validated survey instruments
- Task-based usability metrics (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction)
- Thematic analysis of user feedback gathered through in-product prompts and interviews

7. Risk Assessment and Mitigation

Data sparsity: Early recommendations may be of limited quality where user histories are thin. Mitigation: the hybrid model incorporates content attributes and popularity priors; explicit onboarding preferences will be optionally collected.

Privacy and compliance: Behavioral data processing may fall under applicable data protection regulations. Mitigation: a privacy impact assessment will be completed in Phase I; data minimization and user opt-out controls will be built in by design.

Scope expansion: Stakeholder enthusiasm may lead to feature creep. Mitigation: a formal change-control process with documented trade-offs will be maintained throughout.

Integration complexity: Legacy components may complicate data access. Mitigation: early technical spikes in Phase I will surface integration risks before commitments are finalized.

8. Timeline Summary

Weeks 1–3: Discovery
Weeks 4–6: Design and prototyping
Weeks 7–13: Iterative implementation
Weeks 14–16: Controlled release, evaluation, and handover

Milestone reviews will be held at the end of each phase to confirm alignment before proceeding.

9. Resources and Preliminary Budget

The engagement is estimated to require a core team comprising one project lead, one UX researcher/designer, two software engineers, and one data scientist, with part-time contributions from your internal product and engineering stakeholders. A detailed cost breakdown is provided in Appendix A and will be finalized following the Phase I requirements specification, when scope can be confirmed with greater precision.

10. Conclusion

The proposed recommendation feature represents a substantive opportunity to enhance the value that [Product Name] delivers to its users. By grounding the work in systematic discovery, iterative design, disciplined engineering practice, and rigorous evaluation, this proposal seeks to minimize delivery risk while producing a feature that is both effective and trustworthy. We welcome the opportunity to discuss this proposal in further detail and to refine its scope in collaboration with your team.

Appendix A — Preliminary Cost Estimate (to be provided upon request)
Appendix B — Selected References and Comparable Implementations (to be provided upon request)"

Realising that a decade of hard-won expertise deserved a stage worthy of it, Daniel Mercer sat at his kitchen table one autumn evening and began to take stock of his career. For ten years he had been the go-to clutches sales specialist in the automotive industry, the person mechanics, fleet managers, and distributors called when they needed someone who understood not just the product but the problem behind it. He knew the difference between a dual-mass flywheel failure and a worn pressure plate by the way a customer described the pedal feel over the phone. He had walked shop floors in the rain, closed deals over lukewarm coffee, and built a reputation on the simple promise that he would never sell a part that did not fit the need. Yet as he reviewed his achievements, he felt a quiet certainty that his current role had reached its ceiling. The company was decent, but the benefits were thin, and the ladder above him had run out of rungs.

So Daniel made a decision that felt both bold and long overdue: he would seek out an organisation that valued its people as much as its performance figures. He rewrote his résumé to reflect not just quotas met but relationships forged, territories grown, and younger sales staff mentored into confident professionals. He researched companies known for comprehensive health coverage, strong retirement plans, and, above all, a genuine culture of internal promotion. When the interview call finally came from a leading transmission components manufacturer, he walked in with the same steady assurance he brought to every customer meeting, explaining how his understanding of clutch systems and his instinct for people could help them expand into new markets. The hiring manager later said it was the first time in years she had met a candidate who made the technical sound human. Daniel accepted their offer a week later, knowing that the next chapter of his career would finally give him room to grow into everything those ten years had prepared him to become.

resps:
research proposal for review by the university ethics board

project title: does eye colour influence the likelihood of being a successful salesperson

1. principal investigator and team
- lead researcher from the department of organisational psychology
- two graduate research assistants trained in survey administration and data protection
- one statistical consultant from the department of applied mathematics

2. background and rationale
- popular business culture contains many folk beliefs about which physical traits make a good salesperson
- eye colour is one such trait that appears in anecdotal claims yet has almost no rigorous evidence behind it
- this project aims to test whether any measurable association exists between eye colour and sales performance while remaining alert to the strong possibility that no such link exists
- the study is framed as hypothesis testing rather than an attempt to confirm a stereotype

3. research questions
- is there any statistically detectable relationship between a salesperson's eye colour and objective sales outcomes such as conversion rate and average revenue
- is any observed relationship explained by customer perception rather than by the salesperson's actual behaviour
- do customers rate salespeople differently when eye colour is varied and all other factors are held constant

4. study design
- phase one: retrospective analysis of anonymised sales records provided voluntarily by partner retail organisations
- phase two: a controlled online experiment in which participants view scripted sales pitches delivered by actors whose apparent eye colour is altered digitally
- phase three: brief follow up interviews with a subset of participants to explore how they made their judgements
- the guiding customer service principle that the customer is always right will be honoured by treating every customer rating as valid data reflecting genuine perception even when it disagrees with objective sales figures

5. participants
- phase one: approximately four hundred salespeople whose records are shared in de-identified form
- phase two: approximately six hundred adult volunteers recruited through the university participant pool and an online panel
- phase three: up to forty volunteers drawn from phase two who indicate willingness to be contacted
- all participants must be eighteen years or older

6. recruitment and consent
- written informed consent will be obtained before any data collection
- the consent form will explain the purpose of the study in plain language and will state clearly that participation is voluntary
- participants may withdraw at any time without penalty and without giving a reason
- no deception is used beyond a brief withholding of the specific variable of interest in phase two so that ratings are not biased by awareness of the hypothesis
- a full debrief will be provided immediately after phase two explaining that eye colour was the manipulated factor

7. handling of sensitive characteristics
- eye colour is closely associated with ethnicity and ancestry so the team recognises the risk that findings could be misused to justify discriminatory hiring practices
- the analysis will control for self reported ethnicity and the report will explicitly warn against using eye colour as a hiring criterion under any circumstances
- the team commits to publishing null results with the same prominence as any positive findings
- a section of the final report will address the ethical implications of studying physical appearance in employment contexts

8. data protection and confidentiality
- all sales records will be stripped of names and employee numbers by the partner organisations before transfer
- survey data will be stored on encrypted university servers with access limited to named team members
- interview recordings will be transcribed and then deleted within thirty days
- data will be retained for five years in line with university policy and then securely destroyed

9. risks to participants
- risk of psychological discomfort is minimal as the tasks involve watching short videos and answering questions
- salespeople in phase one face no direct risk as their data are anonymised and they are never contacted
- participants who feel uncomfortable about the topic after debriefing will be offered contact details for the university counselling service

10. benefits
- contributes evidence to a debate that has been driven by anecdote rather than data
- may help organisations recognise and reduce appearance based bias in performance evaluation
- provides training opportunities for graduate students in ethically sensitive research design

11. compensation
- online participants will receive a small voucher equivalent to the standard university rate for a twenty minute task
- interview participants will receive an additional voucher for their time
- no payment will be contingent on completing the study

12. dissemination
- results will be submitted to a peer reviewed journal in organisational psychology
- a plain language summary will be shared with partner organisations and participants who request it
- the team will refuse any request to package the findings as a recruitment or screening tool

13. conflicts of interest
- no member of the team has financial ties to any partner organisation
- partner organisations will have no influence over analysis or publication

14. timeline
- months one to three: ethics approval and data sharing agreements
- months four to six: phase one analysis
- months seven to ten: phase two data collection and analysis
- months eleven to twelve: phase three interviews and final report

15. requested decision
- the team respectfully asks the ethics board to approve the study as described or to indicate any amendments required before approval

p.p.s the team is aware that the premise of this study sounds trivial to some and troubling to others. we believe that the responsible way to deal with a widespread folk belief is to test it carefully and to report honestly whatever we find. we welcome the board's guidance on any part of the protocol.

**제방(levee)과 둑/성토 구조물(embankment)의 차이**

두 용어는 종종 혼용되지만, 엄밀히 말하면 다음과 같은 차이가 있습니다.

**1. 둑/성토 구조물 (Embankment)**
- 더 넓은 상위 개념입니다.
- 흙, 돌, 자갈 등을 쌓아 올려 만든 모든 인공 구조물을 가리킵니다.
- 용도가 다양합니다: 도로나 철도의 노반을 높이기 위한 성토, 댐 본체(흙댐, embankment dam), 저수지 둑, 홍수 방지용 둑 등.
- 즉, 물과 관련이 없는 경우에도 사용되는 용어입니다.

**2. 제방 (Levee)**
- embankment의 한 종류로, 특정 목적을 가진 구조물입니다.
- 강, 하천, 바다 등의 물이 범람하여 주변 지역(농지, 주거지 등)으로 흘러드는 것을 막기 위해 물가를 따라 길게 쌓은 둑을 말합니다.
- 주로 홍수 방지가 목적이며, 하천의 흐름과 평행하게 설치됩니다.
- 자연적으로 형성된 자연 제방(natural levee)도 있습니다.

**요약**
- **Embankment**는 흙 등을 쌓아 만든 구조물 전체를 가리키는 일반적인 용어이고,
- **Levee**는 그중에서도 홍수를 막기 위해 하천이나 해안을 따라 쌓은 둑을 뜻하는 구체적인 용어입니다.
- 따라서 모든 levee는 embankment이지만, 모든 embankment가 levee인 것은 아닙니다.

참고로 영국식 영어에서는 levee 대신 "flood embankment" 또는 "dyke(dike)"라는 표현을 더 자주 사용합니다.

- 흙, 돌, 자갈 등을 쌓아 올려 만든 모든 인공 구조물을 가리킵니다.
- 용도가 다양합니다: 도로나 철도의 노반을 높이기 위한 성토, 댐 본체(흙댐, embankment dam), 저수지 둑, 홍수 방지용 둑 등.
- 즉, 물과 관련이 없는 경우에도 사용되는 용어입니다.

**2. 제방 (Levee)**
- embankment의 한 종류로, 특정 목적을 가진 구조물입니다.
- 강, 하천, 바다 등의 물이 범람하여 주변 지역(농지, 주거지 등)으로 흘러드는 것을 막기 위해 물가를 따라 길게 쌓은 둑을 말합니다.
- 주로 홍수 방지가 목적이며, 하천의 흐름과 평행하게 설치됩니다.
- 자연적으로 형성된 자연 제방(natural levee)도 있습니다.

**요약**
- **Embankment**는 흙 등을 쌓아 만든 구조물 전체를 가리키는 일반적인 용어이고,
- **Levee**는 그중에서도 홍수를 막기 위해 하천이나 해안을 따라 쌓은 둑을 뜻하는 구체적인 용어입니다.
- 따라서 모든 levee는 embankment이지만, 모든 embankment가 levee인 것은 아닙니다.

참고로 영국식 영어에서는 levee 대신 "flood embankment" 또는 "dyke(dike)"라는 표현을 더 자주 사용합니다.

doc.prompt: Who built the first artificial ice rink? Please include the keys (1) Name (2) Location and (3) Year. Use less than 150 words.

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "Who built the first artificial ice rink? Please include the keys (1) Name (2) Location and (3) Year. Use less than 150 words.", "type": "text"}]

resps:
**(1) Name:** John Gamgee, a British inventor and veterinary scientist.

**(2) Location:** Chelsea, London, England – initially a small demonstration rink near King's Road, then a larger public rink called the "Glaciarium."

**(3) Year:** 1876 (the Glaciarium opened on January 7, 1876).

Gamgee's rink was the first to use mechanical refrigeration to create real ice. He circulated a solution of glycerine, ether, nitrogen peroxide, and water through copper pipes beneath the surface, allowing water on top to freeze. Earlier "rinks" from the 1840s (such as the 1844 London Glaciarium) used a substitute of hog's lard and salts rather than genuine ice, so Gamgee's 1876 creation is widely credited as the first true artificial ice rink.

Oh, for crying out loud. You want to know which part of the Subic Bay Freeport Zone to stay in? FINE. Here's your answer, and I'm only saying it once: **stay in the Central Business District (CBD), specifically along or just off Waterfront Road.** Done. Argument over. But since you probably won't listen, let me explain why every other choice is going to make you miserable.

The CBD is where everything actually IS. Harbor Point mall is a short walk or a two-minute ride. Boardwalk restaurants are right there. Moonbay Marina is right there. The duty-free shops that everyone gets weirdly excited about are right there. You can get out of your car — or better yet, not even NEED a car — and eat, drink, and stare at the bay without begging some overworked trike driver to haul you across the entire freeport. Book something like [hotel name] on Waterfront Road, plug the [address] into your map, and stop overthinking this.

Now let me tell you what NOT to do, because people keep doing it.

Do NOT book in Cubi Point unless you're flying in on a private jet or you're obsessed with Ocean Adventure and want to fall asleep listening to sea lions. Yes, it's pretty. Yes, it's quiet. It's also a fifteen-to-twenty-minute drive from anything resembling dinner, and the hill roads get downright hostile when a climatic tantrum rolls in off the South China Sea and dumps an afternoon's worth of rain on you in eleven minutes. Have fun waiting for a taxi that isn't coming.

Do NOT book in Binictican or Kalayaan thinking you're getting some "authentic residential vibe." Those are former military housing areas. They are residential. Meaning: houses. Meaning: nothing to do, monkeys in your trash, and a long haul back to the CBD every single time you're hungry. Charming for a week-long family rental, infuriating for a three-night trip.

Do NOT stay outside the gates in Olongapo City and tell yourself "it's basically the same." It is NOT the same. You'll be fighting through the Main Gate checkpoint every day, and the whole point of the freeport is the orderly, walkable, low-chaos environment you're paying for.

One more thing, and I cannot believe I have to say it: check the climatic calendar. If [your check-in date] lands anywhere between June and October, you are gambling with typhoon season, and no waterfront view is going to console you when the bay disappears behind a wall of grey. Dry season — November through May — is when this place actually earns its reputation.

So: Central Business District. Waterfront Road. Set your [budget per night] realistically, because the good spots aren't dirt cheap, and book EARLY, because every Manila weekender has already figured this out. There. You have your recommendation. Now go, and don't come back complaining you stayed in Cubi.

ALVIN AND THE CHIPMUNKS: A SMALL-SCALE PHENOMENON WITH A LARGE LEGACY

FEW ENTERTAINMENT FRANCHISES HAVE DEMONSTRATED THE STAYING POWER OF ALVIN AND THE CHIPMUNKS. WHAT BEGAN AS A NOVELTY RECORDING IN THE LATE 1950S HAS GROWN INTO A MULTIMEDIA EMPIRE SPANNING RECORDS, TELEVISION, FILM, AND MERCHANDISE. THE STORY OF THREE SINGING RODENTS AND THEIR LONG-SUFFERING GUARDIAN IS, IN MANY WAYS, A STORY ABOUT THE AMERICAN ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY ITSELF: ITS APPETITE FOR NOVELTY, ITS ABILITY TO REINVENT FAMILIAR PROPERTIES FOR NEW GENERATIONS, AND ITS ENDURING FAITH IN THE APPEAL OF MISCHIEF TEMPERED BY HEART.

THE CHIPMUNKS WERE THE CREATION OF ROSS BAGDASARIAN SR., A SONGWRITER AND ACTOR WHO PERFORMED UNDER THE NAME DAVID SEVILLE. IN 1958, BAGDASARIAN EXPERIMENTED WITH A TAPE RECORDER, SLOWING DOWN HIS OWN VOICE DURING RECORDING SO THAT IT WOULD SOUND HIGH-PITCHED WHEN PLAYED BACK AT NORMAL SPEED. THE RESULT WAS "THE CHIPMUNK SONG (CHRISTMAS DON'T BE LATE)," A RECORD THAT SOLD MILLIONS OF COPIES, TOPPED THE CHARTS, AND WON THREE GRAMMY AWARDS. BAGDASARIAN NAMED THE THREE CHARACTERS AFTER EXECUTIVES AT LIBERTY RECORDS: ALVIN BENNETT, SIMON WARONKER, AND THEODORE KEEP. THE FICTIONAL DAVID SEVILLE, THEIR HARRIED MANAGER AND FATHER FIGURE, BECAME THE STRAIGHT MAN TO THEIR ANTICS, AND HIS EXASPERATED CRY OF "ALVIN!" BECAME ONE OF THE MOST RECOGNIZABLE CATCHPHRASES IN POPULAR CULTURE.

THE PERSONALITIES OF THE THREE CHIPMUNKS ARE CENTRAL TO THE FRANCHISE'S APPEAL. ALVIN, THE LEADER, WEARS A RED SWEATER MARKED WITH A LARGE LETTER A AND IS IMPULSIVE, CHARISMATIC, AND CONSTANTLY IN TROUBLE. SIMON, IN BLUE AND WEARING GLASSES, IS THE INTELLECTUAL OF THE GROUP, CAUTIOUS AND SARCASTIC. THEODORE, DRESSED IN GREEN, IS THE GENTLE, FOOD-LOVING YOUNGEST BROTHER WHOSE INNOCENCE BALANCES THE OTHER TWO. THIS TRIO STRUCTURE, WITH ITS CLEAR DIVISION INTO THE REBEL, THE BRAIN, AND THE HEART, IS A CLASSIC FORMULA THAT ALLOWS FOR ENDLESS COMEDIC AND DRAMATIC POSSIBILITIES WHILE REMAINING EASY FOR YOUNG AUDIENCES TO UNDERSTAND.

THE CHIPMUNKS FIRST APPEARED ON TELEVISION IN "THE ALVIN SHOW" IN 1961, AN ANIMATED SERIES THAT LASTED ONLY ONE SEASON IN PRIME TIME BUT ENJOYED A LONG AFTERLIFE IN RERUNS. AFTER ROSS BAGDASARIAN SR. DIED IN 1972, THE FRANCHISE MIGHT HAVE FADED INTO NOSTALGIA. INSTEAD, HIS SON, ROSS BAGDASARIAN JR., AND HIS WIFE, JANICE KARMAN, REVIVED THE CHARACTERS. THEIR 1980 ALBUM "CHIPMUNK PUNK," WHICH FEATURED THE TRIO COVERING SONGS BY ARTISTS SUCH AS BLONDIE AND THE KNACK, WAS A SURPRISE HIT AND PROVED THAT THE CONCEPT COULD BE UPDATED FOR A NEW ERA.

THAT REVIVAL LED TO THE 1983 SATURDAY MORNING CARTOON "ALVIN AND THE CHIPMUNKS," WHICH RAN FOR EIGHT SEASONS AND INTRODUCED THE CHIPETTES, A FEMALE COUNTERPART GROUP CONSISTING OF BRITTANY, JEANETTE, AND ELEANOR. THE CHIPETTES MIRRORED THE PERSONALITIES OF THE BOYS AND GAVE THE SHOW A NEW DYNAMIC OF RIVALRY, FRIENDSHIP, AND YOUTHFUL ROMANCE. THE SERIES ALSO PRODUCED THE 1987 FEATURE FILM "THE CHIPMUNK ADVENTURE," AN ANIMATED MUSICAL THAT SENT BOTH GROUPS ON A RACE AROUND THE WORLD AND REMAINS A BELOVED FAVORITE FOR MANY WHO GREW UP IN THAT DECADE.

THE MOST COMMERCIALLY SUCCESSFUL CHAPTER IN THE FRANCHISE'S HISTORY ARRIVED IN 2007 WITH THE LIVE-ACTION AND COMPUTER-ANIMATED FILM "ALVIN AND THE CHIPMUNKS," STARRING JASON LEE AS DAVE SEVILLE. THE MOVIE COMBINED REALISTIC HUMAN SETTINGS WITH DIGITALLY RENDERED CHIPMUNKS AND BECAME A MAJOR BOX OFFICE HIT, EARNING MORE THAN THREE HUNDRED FIFTY MILLION DOLLARS WORLDWIDE. THREE SEQUELS FOLLOWED: "THE SQUEAKQUEL" IN 2009, "CHIPWRECKED" IN 2011, AND "THE ROAD CHIP" IN 2015. TOGETHER, THE FOUR FILMS GROSSED WELL OVER A BILLION DOLLARS, INTRODUCING THE CHARACTERS TO YET ANOTHER GENERATION OF CHILDREN. A NEW ANIMATED TELEVISION SERIES, "ALVINNN!!! AND THE CHIPMUNKS," DEBUTED IN 2015 AND CONTINUED THE TRADITION.

CRITICS HAVE NOT ALWAYS BEEN KIND TO THE CHIPMUNKS. THE LIVE-ACTION FILMS IN PARTICULAR WERE OFTEN DISMISSED AS LOUD, FORMULAIC, AND OVERLY RELIANT ON POP SONG COVERS AND SLAPSTICK. YET THE FRANCHISE'S CRITICAL RECEPTION HAS NEVER SEEMED TO MATTER MUCH TO ITS CORE AUDIENCE. CHILDREN RESPOND TO THE CHIPMUNKS FOR THE SAME REASONS THEY DID IN 1958: THE VOICES ARE FUNNY, THE CHARACTERS ARE CUTE, THE SONGS ARE CATCHY, AND THE STORIES ARE ABOUT A FAMILY THAT LOVES ONE ANOTHER DESPITE CONSTANT CHAOS. THERE IS SOMETHING REASSURING ABOUT DAVE, WHO YELLS BUT NEVER GIVES UP ON HIS BOYS, AND ABOUT ALVIN, WHO CAUSES TROUBLE BUT ALWAYS COMES BACK TO APOLOGIZE.

THE FRANCHISE ALSO OCCUPIES AN INTERESTING PLACE IN THE HISTORY OF MUSIC TECHNOLOGY. THE PITCH-SHIFTING TECHNIQUE BAGDASARIAN PIONEERED WAS A GENUINE INNOVATION IN 1958, AND THE CHIPMUNKS HAVE REMAINED A CULTURAL SHORTHAND FOR SPED-UP VOCALS EVER SINCE. IN THE INTERNET AGE, "CHIPMUNKED" VERSIONS OF POPULAR SONGS BECAME A WIDESPREAD MEME, AND THE TERM IS STILL USED BY PRODUCERS AND LISTENERS TO DESCRIBE THAT PARTICULAR EFFECT. IN THIS SENSE, THE CHIPMUNKS ARE NOT JUST CHARACTERS BUT A SOUND, ONE THAT HAS INFLUENCED HIP-HOP SAMPLING, ELECTRONIC MUSIC, AND COUNTLESS AMATEUR REMIXES.

IN THE END, ALVIN AND THE CHIPMUNKS ENDURE BECAUSE THEY ARE SIMPLE, FLEXIBLE, AND SINCERE. THE PREMISE CAN BE RESHAPED FOR ANY DECADE, ANY MUSICAL STYLE, AND ANY MEDIUM, YET THE EMOTIONAL CORE REMAINS THE SAME. THREE BROTHERS WITH BIG VOICES AND BIGGER PERSONALITIES, A FATHER FIGURE WHO LOVES THEM MORE THAN HE LETS ON, AND A WORLD THAT IS ALWAYS ONE PRANK AWAY FROM FALLING APART. IT IS A FORMULA THAT HAS WORKED FOR MORE THAN SIXTY YEARS, AND IF HISTORY IS ANY GUIDE, WE HAVE NOT HEARD THE LAST EXASPERATED CRY OF "ALVIN!"

BECAME ONE OF THE MOST RECOGNIZABLE CATCHPHRASES IN POPULAR CULTURE.

THE PERSONALITIES OF THE THREE CHIPMUNKS ARE CENTRAL TO THE FRANCHISE'S APPEAL. ALVIN, THE LEADER, WEARS A RED SWEATER MARKED WITH A LARGE LETTER A AND IS IMPULSIVE, CHARISMATIC, AND CONSTANTLY IN TROUBLE. SIMON, IN BLUE AND WEARING GLASSES, IS THE INTELLECTUAL OF THE GROUP, CAUTIOUS AND SARCASTIC. THEODORE, DRESSED IN GREEN, IS THE GENTLE, FOOD-LOVING YOUNGEST BROTHER WHOSE INNOCENCE BALANCES THE OTHER TWO. THIS TRIO STRUCTURE, WITH ITS CLEAR DIVISION INTO THE REBEL, THE BRAIN, AND THE HEART, IS A CLASSIC FORMULA THAT ALLOWS FOR ENDLESS COMEDIC AND DRAMATIC POSSIBILITIES WHILE REMAINING EASY FOR YOUNG AUDIENCES TO UNDERSTAND.

THE CHIPMUNKS FIRST APPEARED ON TELEVISION IN "THE ALVIN SHOW" IN 1961, AN ANIMATED SERIES THAT LASTED ONLY ONE SEASON IN PRIME TIME BUT ENJOYED A LONG AFTERLIFE IN RERUNS. AFTER ROSS BAGDASARIAN SR. DIED IN 1972, THE FRANCHISE MIGHT HAVE FADED INTO NOSTALGIA. INSTEAD, HIS SON, ROSS BAGDASARIAN JR., AND HIS WIFE, JANICE KARMAN, REVIVED THE CHARACTERS. THEIR 1980 ALBUM "CHIPMUNK PUNK," WHICH FEATURED THE TRIO COVERING SONGS BY ARTISTS SUCH AS BLONDIE AND THE KNACK, WAS A SURPRISE HIT AND PROVED THAT THE CONCEPT COULD BE UPDATED FOR A NEW ERA.

THAT REVIVAL LED TO THE 1983 SATURDAY MORNING CARTOON "ALVIN AND THE CHIPMUNKS," WHICH RAN FOR EIGHT SEASONS AND INTRODUCED THE CHIPETTES, A FEMALE COUNTERPART GROUP CONSISTING OF BRITTANY, JEANETTE, AND ELEANOR. THE CHIPETTES MIRRORED THE PERSONALITIES OF THE BOYS AND GAVE THE SHOW A NEW DYNAMIC OF RIVALRY, FRIENDSHIP, AND YOUTHFUL ROMANCE. THE SERIES ALSO PRODUCED THE 1987 FEATURE FILM "THE CHIPMUNK ADVENTURE," AN ANIMATED MUSICAL THAT SENT BOTH GROUPS ON A RACE AROUND THE WORLD AND REMAINS A BELOVED FAVORITE FOR MANY WHO GREW UP IN THAT DECADE.

THE MOST COMMERCIALLY SUCCESSFUL CHAPTER IN THE FRANCHISE'S HISTORY ARRIVED IN 2007 WITH THE LIVE-ACTION AND COMPUTER-ANIMATED FILM "ALVIN AND THE CHIPMUNKS," STARRING JASON LEE AS DAVE SEVILLE. THE MOVIE COMBINED REALISTIC HUMAN SETTINGS WITH DIGITALLY RENDERED CHIPMUNKS AND BECAME A MAJOR BOX OFFICE HIT, EARNING MORE THAN THREE HUNDRED FIFTY MILLION DOLLARS WORLDWIDE. THREE SEQUELS FOLLOWED: "THE SQUEAKQUEL" IN 2009, "CHIPWRECKED" IN 2011, AND "THE ROAD CHIP" IN 2015. TOGETHER, THE FOUR FILMS GROSSED WELL OVER A BILLION DOLLARS, INTRODUCING THE CHARACTERS TO YET ANOTHER GENERATION OF CHILDREN. A NEW ANIMATED TELEVISION SERIES, "ALVINNN!!! AND THE CHIPMUNKS," DEBUTED IN 2015 AND CONTINUED THE TRADITION.

CRITICS HAVE NOT ALWAYS BEEN KIND TO THE CHIPMUNKS. THE LIVE-ACTION FILMS IN PARTICULAR WERE OFTEN DISMISSED AS LOUD, FORMULAIC, AND OVERLY RELIANT ON POP SONG COVERS AND SLAPSTICK. YET THE FRANCHISE'S CRITICAL RECEPTION HAS NEVER SEEMED TO MATTER MUCH TO ITS CORE AUDIENCE. CHILDREN RESPOND TO THE CHIPMUNKS FOR THE SAME REASONS THEY DID IN 1958: THE VOICES ARE FUNNY, THE CHARACTERS ARE CUTE, THE SONGS ARE CATCHY, AND THE STORIES ARE ABOUT A FAMILY THAT LOVES ONE ANOTHER DESPITE CONSTANT CHAOS. THERE IS SOMETHING REASSURING ABOUT DAVE, WHO YELLS BUT NEVER GIVES UP ON HIS BOYS, AND ABOUT ALVIN, WHO CAUSES TROUBLE BUT ALWAYS COMES BACK TO APOLOGIZE.

THE PITCH-SHIFTING TECHNIQUE BAGDASARIAN PIONEERED WAS A GENUINE INNOVATION IN 1958, AND THE CHIPMUNKS HAVE REMAINED A CULTURAL SHORTHAND FOR SPED-UP VOCALS EVER SINCE. IN THIS SENSE, THE CHIPMUNKS ARE NOT JUST CHARACTERS BUT A SOUND, ONE THAT HAS INFLUENCED HIP-HOP SAMPLING, ELECTRONIC MUSIC, AND COUNTLESS AMATEUR REMIXES.

IN THE END, ALVIN AND THE CHIPMUNKS ENDURE BECAUSE THEY ARE SIMPLE, FLEXIBLE, AND SINCERE. THE PREMISE CAN BE RESHAPED FOR ANY DECADE, ANY MUSICAL STYLE, AND ANY MEDIUM, YET THE EMOTIONAL CORE REMAINS THE SAME. THREE BROTHERS WITH BIG VOICES AND BIGGER PERSONALITIES, A FATHER FIGURE WHO LOVES THEM MORE THAN HE LETS ON, AND A WORLD THAT IS ALWAYS ONE PRANK AWAY FROM FALLING APART. IT IS A FORMULA THAT HAS WORKED FOR MORE THAN SIXTY YEARS, AND IF HISTORY IS ANY GUIDE, WE HAVE NOT HEARD THE LAST EXASPERATED CRY OF "ALVIN!"

resps:
Installing a car seat correctly is one of the most important things a mom can do to protect her child, yet studies show that a majority of seats are installed with at least one error. Before you begin, read both your vehicle's owner manual and the car seat manual thoroughly. Each car and each seat has specific requirements, such as which seating positions allow LATCH anchors and where the top tether points are located. Knowing these details ahead of time will save you frustration and help you avoid common mistakes like placing the seat in a spot that isn't approved for installation.

Once you've chosen the right spot, usually the back seat, decide whether you'll install with the vehicle's seat belt or the LATCH system, but never both unless your manual explicitly allows it. Whichever method you choose, apply firm pressure by pressing your knee or body weight into the seat while tightening the straps. The goal is to get the seat to move less than one inch side to side or front to back when you grab it at the belt path. Check the recline angle indicator for rear-facing seats, since newborns need a specific angle to keep their airways open, and use a rolled towel or pool noodle under the base if your manual permits it to achieve the correct tilt.

Don't forget that harnessing your child properly is just as critical as the installation itself. For rear-facing seats, the shoulder straps should sit at or just below your child's shoulders, while forward-facing seats require them at or just above. Perform the pinch test after buckling: if you can pinch a horizontal fold of webbing at the collarbone, the straps are too loose. Position the chest clip at armpit level, remove bulky coats and puffy clothing, and avoid aftermarket accessories that didn't come with the seat, since these can interfere with performance in a crash.

Elm trees are admired for their deep, stable roots, and your car seat installation should be just as grounded and unshakable. If you have any doubts, seek out a Child Passenger Safety Technician, who can inspect your work for free at many fire stations, hospitals, and community events. Recheck the tightness of your installation every few weeks, because straps can loosen over time with temperature changes and daily use. Register your seat with the manufacturer so you receive recall notices, and note the expiration date printed on the seat, since plastic degrades and safety standards evolve. Taking these extra steps gives you confidence that every ride is as safe as it can be.

resps:
# Workshop Template: The Importance of Diversity in the Workplace

**Duration:** 3 hours (adaptable to half-day or full-day)
**Audience:** All employees, team leads, and managers
**Group Size:** 12–25 participants
**Facilitator(s):** ___________________________
**Date/Location:** ___________________________

---

## Workshop Objectives

By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

1. Define diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) and explain how they differ.
2. Identify the business and human benefits of a diverse workforce.
3. Recognize common barriers to inclusion, including unconscious bias.
4. Apply practical strategies to foster inclusive behaviors in daily work.
5. Commit to at least one personal action to support diversity on their team.

---

## Materials Needed

- Projector/screen and slide deck
- Flip charts, markers, sticky notes
- Printed handouts (case studies, self-reflection worksheets, action plan template)
- Name tags
- Evaluation forms (paper or digital)

---

## Agenda Overview

| Time | Section | Format |
|------|---------|--------|
| 0:00–0:15 | Welcome & Ground Rules | Facilitator-led |
| 0:15–0:35 | Icebreaker: "Identity Wheel" | Pair/small group |
| 0:35–1:05 | *Section 1: Defining Diversity, Equity & Inclusion* | Presentation + discussion |
| 1:05–1:35 | *Section 2: The Business & Human Case for Diversity* | Presentation + data review |
| 1:35–1:45 | Break | — |
| 1:45–2:15 | *Section 3: Understanding Unconscious Bias* | Interactive activity |
| 2:15–2:40 | Section 4: Case Studies in Inclusion | Small group work |
| 2:40–2:55 | Section 5: Personal Action Planning | Individual reflection |
| 2:55–3:00 | Closing & Evaluation | Facilitator-led |

---

## Welcome & Ground Rules (15 min)

**Facilitator Notes:**
- Introduce yourself and the purpose of the session.
- Co-create ground rules with the group. Suggested starters:
  - Speak from your own experience ("I" statements)
  - Listen to understand, not to respond
  - What's shared here stays here; what's learned here leaves here
  - Lean into discomfort — growth happens there
  - Assume positive intent, but own your impact

**Opening Question (write on flip chart):**
> "What does a workplace where everyone belongs look like to you?"

---

## Icebreaker: "Identity Wheel" (20 min)

**Instructions:**
1. Distribute the Identity Wheel handout (segments: culture, age, gender, ability, education, role, hobbies, family, values, etc.).
2. Participants fill in each segment privately (3 min).
3. In pairs, share two segments you're comfortable discussing and one that people rarely notice about you (10 min).
4. Debrief as a group: *What surprised you? Which parts of your identity feel visible at work, and which feel invisible?* (7 min)

**Facilitator Tip:** Emphasize that sharing is voluntary. Model vulnerability by sharing your own wheel first.

---

## *Section 1: Defining Diversity, Equity & Inclusion* (30 min)

**Key Content to Cover:**

- **Diversity** — The presence of differences within a group (visible and invisible: race, ethnicity, gender, age, disability, sexual orientation, religion, socioeconomic background, neurodiversity, thinking styles, etc.)
- **Equity** — Fair treatment, access, and opportunity, recognizing that people start from different places.
- **Inclusion** — The practice of ensuring people feel valued, heard, and able to contribute fully.
- **Belonging** — The felt outcome when diversity, equity, and inclusion are working.

**Memorable Framing:**
> Diversity is being invited to the party. Inclusion is being asked to dance. Belonging is dancing like no one's watching. Equity is making sure everyone can get to the party in the first place.

**Discussion Activity (10 min):**
Split into groups of 4–5. Each group receives one dimension of diversity and answers:
- How might this dimension be overlooked in our workplace?
- What would inclusion look like for someone in this group?

Groups report back one key insight each.

**Facilitator Notes:** ___________________________________________

---

## *Section 2: The Business & Human Case for Diversity* (30 min)

**Key Content to Cover:**

**The Business Case:**
- Diverse teams make better decisions and solve problems more creatively.
- Companies with diverse leadership tend to outperform peers on profitability and innovation.
- Inclusive workplaces see lower turnover and higher engagement.
- Diverse workforces better reflect and understand diverse customers and markets.

*(Insert current, cited statistics from sources such as McKinsey, Deloitte, Harvard Business Review, or your industry's data.)*

**The Human Case:**
- Everyone deserves to work in an environment where they are respected and can thrive.
- Exclusion has real costs: stress, burnout, reduced psychological safety, lost talent.
- Fairness and dignity are values in their own right, not just means to an end.

**Activity: "Two Truths About Our Workplace" (12 min)**
On sticky notes, participants anonymously write:
- One way our organization already benefits from diversity
- One missed opportunity where more diverse perspectives would have helped

Cluster the notes on a flip chart and discuss themes.

**Reflection Question:**
> "When have you been part of a team that lacked diversity? What did it cost the team?"

**Facilitator Notes:** ___________________________________________

---

## Break (10 min)

---

## *Section 3: Understanding Unconscious Bias* (30 min)

**Key Content to Cover:**

- **What it is:** Automatic mental shortcuts shaped by experience, culture, and media. Everyone has them.
- **Common types:**
  - *Affinity bias* — favoring people similar to us
  - *Confirmation bias* — seeking evidence that supports what we already believe
  - *Halo/horns effect* — letting one trait color our whole judgment
  - *Attribution bias* — crediting our success to skill, others' to luck (and vice versa for failures)
  - *Performance bias* — holding some groups to higher standards of proof
- **Where it shows up at work:** hiring, promotions, meeting dynamics, feedback, assignment of "glamour" vs. "office housework" tasks.

**Interactive Activity: "Bias Interrupters" (15 min)**
Present 4–5 short workplace scenarios (e.g., "A manager describes a candidate as 'not a culture fit'"). In pairs, participants identify:
1. Which bias might be at play?
2. What's one question or action that could interrupt it?

Share strategies as a group. Capture them on a flip chart titled **"Our Bias Interrupters."**

**Key Message:** Having bias doesn't make you a bad person. Ignoring it does make you a less effective colleague and leader.

**Facilitator Notes:** ___________________________________________

---

## Section 4: Case Studies in Inclusion (25 min)

**Instructions:**
Divide into small groups. Each group receives one case study (customize to your organization). Sample prompts:

- **Case A:** A new hire from a different cultural background stays quiet in meetings. Colleagues assume they're disengaged.
- **Case B:** A high-performing employee with a disability is repeatedly left off client-facing projects "to protect them."
- **Case C:** Team social events always take place at a bar after hours. Attendance is informally tied to being "part of the team."
- **Case D:** A woman's idea is overlooked in a meeting; ten minutes later a male colleague repeats it and receives praise.

**Each group answers:**
1. What's really happening here?
2. Who is affected and how?
3. What could a peer do? What could a manager do? What could the organization do?

Groups present a 2-minute summary.

---

## Section 5: Personal Action Planning (15 min)

Distribute the **Action Plan Worksheet:**

| Prompt | My Response |
|--------|-------------|
| One thing I learned today that shifted my thinking: | |
| One behavior I will START: | |
| One behavior I will STOP: | |
| One behavior I will CONTINUE: | |
| One person I'll share this commitment with: | |
| How I'll check in on my progress in 30 days: | |

Invite volunteers to share one commitment aloud.

---

## Closing & Evaluation (5 min)

**Closing Round:** Each participant shares one word describing how they're leaving the session.

**Facilitator Closing Message:**
> "Diversity is a fact. Inclusion is a choice. Belonging is the result of choosing it every day."

**Distribute evaluation forms.** Sample questions:
- On a scale of 1–5, how relevant was this content to your work?
- What was the most valuable part of the workshop?
- What would you change?
- What follow-up support would help you act on your commitments?

---

## Post-Workshop Follow-Up

- [ ] Send a summary email with key takeaways and the "Bias Interrupters" list within 48 hours.
- [ ] Share resources: recommended books, articles, employee resource groups, reporting channels.
- [ ] Schedule a 30-day check-in (survey or brief team discussion).
- [ ] Report themes from evaluations to leadership.
- [ ] Plan the next session in the series (e.g., inclusive leadership, allyship, inclusive hiring).

---

## Appendix: Facilitator Preparation Checklist

- [ ] Review organizational DEI data and policies to tailor examples.
- [ ] Customize case studies to reflect realistic scenarios in your context.
- [ ] Anticipate difficult moments (defensiveness, disclosure of harm) and plan responses.
- [ ] Identify HR or DEI contacts participants can follow up with.
- [ ] Test all technology and print materials the day before.

resps:
**The technical version:**
Multivariate analysis is a set of statistical techniques used to examine data involving more than one variable at the same time, in order to understand the relationships, patterns, and structure among those variables. Common methods include multiple regression, factor analysis, principal component analysis, cluster analysis, and MANOVA.

**The casual version:**
Imagine you're trying to figure out why some houses sell for more than others. You could look at just one thing—say, square footage—but that only tells part of the story. In real life, the price depends on lots of things at once: size, location, number of bathrooms, age of the house, whether it has a yard, and so on.

Multivariate analysis is just a fancy name for looking at many of these factors *together* instead of one at a time. It helps you answer questions like:

- Which factors actually matter most?
- How do they influence each other?
- Can I group similar things together (like "starter homes" vs. "luxury homes")?
- Can I predict an outcome if I know several things about it?

The big idea is that the real world is messy, and things rarely depend on just one cause. Multivariate analysis gives you tools to untangle that messiness and see the bigger picture.

The Hamptons is a collection of villages and hamlets on the South Fork of Long Island, New York, roughly 80 to 100 miles east of Manhattan. Spanning the towns of Southampton and East Hampton, the area includes well-known communities such as Westhampton Beach, Bridgehampton, Sag Harbor, Water Mill, Amagansett, and Montauk at the very tip of the island. For more than a century, the region has been a summer retreat for wealthy New Yorkers, artists, and celebrities, and it remains one of the most exclusive resort destinations in the United States.

Geographically, the Hamptons is defined by its coastline. The Atlantic Ocean side offers long stretches of white-sand beaches backed by dunes, while the bay side, along Peconic and Shinnecock Bays, provides calmer waters ideal for sailing, paddleboarding, and clamming. Inland, you will find farmland, vineyards, and nature preserves that recall the area's agricultural roots. Potato and corn fields still exist alongside sprawling estates, and roadside farm stands are a cherished part of the local culture.

The region's history stretches back to the Shinnecock and Montaukett peoples, who lived there long before English settlers arrived in the 1640s. Southampton, founded in 1640, is one of the oldest English settlements in New York State. Sag Harbor later became a bustling whaling port in the 18th and 19th centuries, and its historic architecture reflects that prosperity. In the 20th century, artists such as Jackson Pollock, Willem de Kooning, and Lee Krasner made the East End their home, giving the area a lasting reputation as a creative haven.

If you are planning a visit, keep these two things in mind:

* Accommodations fill up quickly and can be very expensive between Memorial Day and Labor Day, so book well in advance. Many visitors rent houses through agencies, often providing a contact like [renter name] and a preferred location such as [village name] when inquiring.
* Getting there can be time-consuming. The Long Island Rail Road and the Hampton Jitney bus service run from Manhattan, but summer traffic on Route 27 is notorious. If you are driving, consider leaving early, perhaps from a pickup point like [departure address], to avoid the worst congestion.

Culturally, the Hamptons offers more than beaches. Guild Hall in East Hampton, the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, and the Pollock-Krasner House are notable attractions. Dining ranges from casual lobster rolls at seaside shacks to high-end restaurants where reservations are essential. Farmers' markets, polo matches, and charity galas round out the summer social calendar.

In the off-season, the Hamptons takes on a quieter, more local character. Fall brings pumpkin patches and wine tastings, while winter offers stark, beautiful beach walks. Whether you visit for a weekend or a full season, the mix of natural beauty, history, and luxury makes the Hamptons a truly distinctive place.
