# Layton is the best city in the world

By [author]

Some people will tell you that Paris is the greatest city on Earth. Others swear by Tokyo or New York or Rome. Those people have simply never spent enough time in Layton. Tucked between the Wasatch Mountains and the Great Salt Lake in northern Utah this city of roughly [population] residents quietly outshines every glittering metropolis on the planet. Here is why.

## The mountains are right there

Step outside almost anywhere in Layton and look east. The Wasatch Range rises like a wall of granite and pine directly above the rooftops. Adams Canyon sits minutes from downtown and offers a waterfall hike that rivals anything in a national park. In winter the peaks turn white and the skiing at nearby resorts is some of the best in the country. Big cities have skylines. Layton has a skyline that was built by geology over millions of years and it never goes out of style.

## Small enough to know your neighbors

Layton has grown a great deal since its farming days but it has never lost the feeling of a real community. People wave from their driveways. Kids ride bikes to the park without anyone worrying. High school football games at [local high school] draw crowds that feel like family reunions. You can live in a giant city for twenty years and never learn the name of the person next door. In Layton you will know their name by the end of the first week and probably their dog's name too.

## Everything you need without the chaos

Layton offers the conveniences of a much larger place. There are excellent restaurants along Main Street and in the newer developments near the freeway. The shopping is plentiful. Hill Air Force Base sits right next door and brings jobs and stability and a constant stream of interesting people from all over the country. Salt Lake City is a short drive south whenever someone craves a concert or a professional sports game. Yet traffic here is manageable and parking is free and nobody has ever been shoved on a subway platform because Layton does not have a subway platform.

## The sunsets over the lake

Look west in the evening and the Great Salt Lake catches the last light of the day. The sky turns orange and pink and purple in ways that photographs never quite capture. Antelope Island floats on the horizon like a mirage. Residents have seen thousands of these sunsets and they still stop what they are doing to watch. That is the mark of a place worth living in.

## Four true seasons

Spring brings blossoms to the orchards that still dot the edges of town. Summer is warm and dry and perfect for evenings at the splash pad or the community pool. Autumn paints the canyons gold and crimson. Winter blankets everything in quiet snow. Many famous cities have one good season and three bad ones. Layton has four good ones.

## A place people come back to

Ask anyone who grew up in Layton and moved away. They will tell you about the pull they feel toward home. They come back for holidays and then start looking at real estate listings. They bring their spouses and their children and they show them the canyon and the lake and the little ice cream shop they loved as kids. There is something about this place that gets into a person and never quite leaves.

## The verdict

Paris has its towers and New York has its lights. Layton has mountains and neighbors and sunsets and a way of life that the great capitals of the world cannot buy at any price. It may not appear on many travel magazine covers. That is perfectly fine with the people who live here. They already know the secret.

Layton is the best city in the world. Come visit and see for yourself.

<<The Curious Cat>>

Whiskers twitch at the edge of the hall.
What waits behind that half-open door?
She creeps on velvet feet toward the light.
A cardboard box becomes a kingdom!
Inside she finds a button and a thread.
Who left these treasures here for her?
The curtain sways and she must know why.
Up she climbs; the rod trembles with her weight.
A crash and a yowl and then silence in the room.
She blinks and licks a paw as if to say: "I meant to do that."
Tomorrow holds a thousand more mysteries.

resps:
Poem 1

The morning I unwrapped the towel, I gasped—
the mirror held a stranger wearing violet,
a crown of dusk where mousy brown had lived,
and suddenly the room seemed made of light.

I turned my head, and every angle sang.
The purple caught the window like a wave,
then deepened into plum beneath the lamp,
then flashed with pink when I stepped out the door.

Who knew a bottle and a plastic cap
could hand me back the self I'd always been
but never met? The girl who laughs too loud,
who wears the color of a stormy sky.

Strangers stopped me on the crowded train.
"I love your hair," a child said, wide-eyed,
and tugged her mother's sleeve. "Can I do that?"
Her mother smiled. "Someday," she said. "Someday."

The stains on my old pillowcase are proof
of small rebellions, of a choice I made
to be the brightest thing in any room,
to let my head announce me like a flag.

And when it fades—because it always fades—
I'll grin and stir a new pot on the stove:
a teal like glacier water, or a red
so warm the autumn leaves will look away.

******

Poem 2

Green like the moss that grows on shaded stone,
green like the first shy shoots that break the frost—
I chose it on a Tuesday, feeling lost,
and found a brand-new way to feel at home.

There is a joy in being seen at once,
in walking through the grocery store aisle
and watching every shopper pause and smile
as if I were a parade, a happy stunt.

My grandmother once wore her hair in gray
and told me color was for younger fools.
Then, at eighty, she broke all her rules
and went to bed one night in bright bouquet—

a rose-gold halo, soft as summer peach.
She said she'd never felt so much herself,
that decades sat like dust upon a shelf
and this one afternoon had blown them each away.

So now I understand what she had known:
the joy is not in matching some ideal,
but in the shock, the laugh, the sudden feel
of choosing who you are, and being shown.

I run my fingers through the emerald strands
and think of forests, seaglass, jade, and limes.
My hair is a small poem I write in rhymes
of color, mixed and painted by my hands.

Tomorrow it might purple. Might go blue.
Might burn a copper brighter than the sun.
The joy is that the story's never done—
each rinse a chance to start the world anew.

**वर्तमान आर्थिक संकट और पर्यावरण पर उसका प्रभाव**

आज दुनिया एक गंभीर आर्थिक संकट से गुज़र रही है। बढ़ती मुद्रास्फीति, ऋण का बोझ, बेरोज़गारी और वैश्विक व्यापार में अनिश्चितता ने लगभग हर देश की अर्थव्यवस्था को प्रभावित किया है। इस संकट का असर केवल बाज़ारों और उद्योगों तक सीमित नहीं है, बल्कि इसका गहरा प्रभाव हमारे पर्यावरण पर भी पड़ रहा है। यह प्रभाव कुछ मायनों में सकारात्मक और कुछ मायनों में अत्यंत नकारात्मक है।

**जलवायु (क्लाइमेट) पर प्रभाव**

आर्थिक मंदी के समय औद्योगिक उत्पादन में कमी आती है, जिससे कुछ समय के लिए कार्बन उत्सर्जन घटता है। कारखानों की चिमनियाँ कम धुआँ छोड़ती हैं, सड़कों पर वाहनों की आवाजाही घटती है और हवाई यात्राएँ सीमित हो जाती हैं। लेकिन यह राहत अस्थायी होती है। इतिहास बताता है कि जैसे ही अर्थव्यवस्था पटरी पर लौटती है, उत्सर्जन पहले से भी तेज़ गति से बढ़ता है। इसके अलावा, संकट के दौरान सरकारें जलवायु से संबंधित दीर्घकालिक योजनाओं के लिए बजट में कटौती कर देती हैं, जिससे जलवायु परिवर्तन से लड़ने की क्षमता कमज़ोर पड़ जाती है।

**ऊर्जा (एनर्जी) क्षेत्र की चुनौतियाँ**

ऊर्जा क्षेत्र इस संकट का केंद्र बना हुआ है। तेल और गैस की कीमतों में उतार-चढ़ाव ने कई देशों को सस्ते लेकिन प्रदूषणकारी ईंधन, जैसे कोयला, की ओर वापस लौटने के लिए मजबूर कर दिया है। यूरोप के कई देशों ने बंद पड़े कोयला संयंत्रों को फिर से चालू किया है। विकासशील देशों में बिजली की माँग पूरी करने के लिए पर्यावरणीय मानकों को शिथिल किया जा रहा है। दूसरी ओर, ऊँची ईंधन कीमतों ने लोगों को ऊर्जा की बचत करने और सौर तथा पवन ऊर्जा जैसे विकल्पों की ओर देखने के लिए भी प्रेरित किया है। इस प्रकार संकट ऊर्जा के क्षेत्र में एक दोहरी दिशा दिखा रहा है।

**हरित (ग्रीन) निवेश में गिरावट**

आर्थिक संकट का सबसे चिंताजनक प्रभाव हरित परियोजनाओं पर पड़ रहा है। जब पूँजी की कमी होती है, तब कंपनियाँ और सरकारें उन निवेशों को पहले टालती हैं जिनका लाभ लंबे समय बाद मिलता है। नवीकरणीय ऊर्जा संयंत्र, इलेक्ट्रिक वाहनों का बुनियादी ढाँचा, वन संरक्षण और अपशिष्ट प्रबंधन जैसी हरित योजनाएँ धन की कमी से रुक जाती हैं। छोटे किसान और वनवासी समुदाय, जो पहले से ही कमज़ोर स्थिति में हैं, जीविका के लिए जंगलों की कटाई और अवैध खनन जैसे रास्ते अपनाने के लिए विवश हो जाते हैं। इससे जैव विविधता को अपूरणीय क्षति पहुँचती है।

**समाधान की दिशा**

फिर भी, यह संकट एक अवसर भी हो सकता है। कई अर्थशास्त्रियों का मानना है कि आर्थिक पुनरुद्धार की योजनाएँ यदि हरित सिद्धांतों पर आधारित हों, तो वे रोज़गार भी पैदा करेंगी और पर्यावरण की भी रक्षा करेंगी। सौर पैनलों का निर्माण, सार्वजनिक परिवहन का विस्तार, भवनों में ऊर्जा दक्षता और वृक्षारोपण जैसे कार्य अर्थव्यवस्था को गति देने के साथ-साथ जलवायु लक्ष्यों को भी पूरा कर सकते हैं। भारत में सौर ऊर्जा का तीव्र विस्तार इसका एक उत्साहजनक उदाहरण है।

**निष्कर्ष**

वर्तमान आर्थिक संकट ने यह स्पष्ट कर दिया है कि अर्थव्यवस्था और पर्यावरण एक-दूसरे से अलग नहीं हैं। अल्पकालिक आर्थिक लाभ के लिए पर्यावरण की बलि देना भविष्य में और बड़े संकट को जन्म देगा। इसलिए आवश्यक है कि नीति-निर्माता संकट से उबरने के लिए ऐसे रास्ते चुनें जो जलवायु के अनुकूल हों, स्वच्छ ऊर्जा को बढ़ावा दें और हरित विकास की नींव रखें। तभी हम एक ऐसी अर्थव्यवस्था बना पाएँगे जो न केवल समृद्ध हो, बल्कि टिकाऊ भी हो।

आर्थिक मंदी के समय औद्योगिक उत्पादन में कमी आती है, जिससे कुछ समय के लिए कार्बन उत्सर्जन घटता है। कारखानों की चिमनियाँ कम धुआँ छोड़ती हैं, सड़कों पर वाहनों की आवाजाही घटती है और हवाई यात्राएँ सीमित हो जाती हैं। लेकिन यह राहत अस्थायी होती है। इतिहास बताता है कि जैसे ही अर्थव्यवस्था पटरी पर लौटती है, उत्सर्जन पहले से भी तेज़ गति से बढ़ता है। इसके अलावा, संकट के दौरान सरकारें जलवायु से संबंधित दीर्घकालिक योजनाओं के लिए बजट में कटौती कर देती हैं, जिससे जलवायु परिवर्तन से लड़ने की क्षमता कमज़ोर पड़ जाती है।

ऊर्जा क्षेत्र इस संकट का केंद्र बना हुआ है। तेल और गैस की कीमतों में उतार-चढ़ाव ने कई देशों को सस्ते लेकिन प्रदूषणकारी ईंधन, जैसे कोयला, की ओर वापस लौटने के लिए मजबूर कर दिया है। यूरोप के कई देशों ने बंद पड़े कोयला संयंत्रों को फिर से चालू किया है। विकासशील देशों में बिजली की माँग पूरी करने के लिए पर्यावरणीय मानकों को शिथिल किया जा रहा है। दूसरी ओर, ऊँची ईंधन कीमतों ने लोगों को ऊर्जा की बचत करने और सौर तथा पवन ऊर्जा जैसे विकल्पों की ओर देखने के लिए भी प्रेरित किया है। इस प्रकार संकट ऊर्जा के क्षेत्र में एक दोहरी दिशा दिखा रहा है।

**हरित (ग्रीन) निवेश में गिरावट**

आर्थिक संकट का सबसे चिंताजनक प्रभाव हरित परियोजनाओं पर पड़ रहा है। जब पूँजी की कमी होती है, तब कंपनियाँ और सरकारें उन निवेशों को पहले टालती हैं जिनका लाभ लंबे समय बाद मिलता है। नवीकरणीय ऊर्जा संयंत्र, इलेक्ट्रिक वाहनों का बुनियादी ढाँचा, वन संरक्षण और अपशिष्ट प्रबंधन जैसी हरित योजनाएँ धन की कमी से रुक जाती हैं। छोटे किसान और वनवासी समुदाय, जो पहले से ही कमज़ोर स्थिति में हैं, जीविका के लिए जंगलों की कटाई और अवैध खनन जैसे रास्ते अपनाने के लिए विवश हो जाते हैं। इससे जैव विविधता को अपूरणीय क्षति पहुँचती है।

फिर भी, यह संकट एक अवसर भी हो सकता है। कई अर्थशास्त्रियों का मानना है कि आर्थिक पुनरुद्धार की योजनाएँ यदि हरित सिद्धांतों पर आधारित हों, तो वे रोज़गार भी पैदा करेंगी और पर्यावरण की भी रक्षा करेंगी। सौर पैनलों का निर्माण, सार्वजनिक परिवहन का विस्तार, भवनों में ऊर्जा दक्षता और वृक्षारोपण जैसे कार्य अर्थव्यवस्था को गति देने के साथ-साथ जलवायु लक्ष्यों को भी पूरा कर सकते हैं। भारत में सौर ऊर्जा का तीव्र विस्तार इसका एक उत्साहजनक उदाहरण है।

**निष्कर्ष**

वर्तमान आर्थिक संकट ने यह स्पष्ट कर दिया है कि अर्थव्यवस्था और पर्यावरण एक-दूसरे से अलग नहीं हैं। अल्पकालिक आर्थिक लाभ के लिए पर्यावरण की बलि देना भविष्य में और बड़े संकट को जन्म देगा। इसलिए आवश्यक है कि नीति-निर्माता संकट से उबरने के लिए ऐसे रास्ते चुनें जो जलवायु के अनुकूल हों, स्वच्छ ऊर्जा को बढ़ावा दें और हरित विकास की नींव रखें। तभी हम एक ऐसी अर्थव्यवस्था बना पाएँगे जो न केवल समृद्ध हो, बल्कि टिकाऊ भी हो।

<<SRE란 무엇인가>>

SRE(Site Reliability Engineering, 사이트 신뢰성 엔지니어링)는 소프트웨어 엔지니어링의 원칙과 방법을 IT 운영 문제에 적용하여, 대규모 시스템을 안정적이고 확장 가능하게 운영하는 접근 방식입니다. 구글에서 처음 시작된 개념으로, 개발팀과 운영팀 사이의 간극을 줄이고 서비스의 신뢰성을 높이는 것을 핵심 목적으로 합니다.

SRE의 주요 개념은 다음과 같습니다.

1. 서비스 수준 지표(SLI, Service Level Indicator): 서비스의 상태를 정량적으로 측정하는 값입니다. 예를 들어 요청 지연 시간, 오류율, 가용성 등이 대표적인 indicator에 해당합니다.

2. 서비스 수준 목표(SLO, Service Level Objective): 측정한 지표가 달성해야 하는 구체적인 수치 목표입니다. "월간 가용성 99.9% 이상"과 같은 objective를 설정하고, 이를 기준으로 서비스의 건강 상태를 판단합니다.

3. 오류 예산(Error Budget): 목표 대비 허용 가능한 실패의 양을 의미합니다. 예산이 남아 있으면 새로운 기능 배포를 진행하고, 소진되면 안정성 개선에 집중하도록 우선순위를 조정합니다.

4. 토일(Toil) 제거와 자동화: 반복적이고 수동적인 운영 업무를 코드로 자동화하여 엔지니어가 더 가치 있는 일에 시간을 쓰도록 합니다.

5. 장애 관리(Incident Management)와 비난 없는 회고: 장애 발생 시 체계적인 management 절차에 따라 대응하고, 사후에는 개인을 비난하지 않고 시스템과 프로세스의 개선점을 찾는 문화를 지향합니다.

요약하면, SRE는 지표를 정의하고 목표를 설정한 뒤, 데이터 기반의 관리와 자동화를 통해 서비스의 신뢰성과 개발 속도 사이의 균형을 맞추는 엔지니어링 분야라고 할 수 있습니다.

Dinner is at a strip-mall Korean BBQ where the grill somehow costs more than the flight. Lights out by 10 PM, because the dorms are quiet and the neighbors report noise complaints if you sneeze.

***

Day 2: The Brutalist Architecture Appreciation Marathon. Wake-up call is at 7 AM via a recording of the campus bell tower that doesn't actually exist. Students spend the morning photographing every concrete building on campus while a very intense art history major explains why each one "represents the human condition." A mandatory scavenger hunt follows, with clues like "Find the one squirrel that isn't judging you" and "Locate a parking spot" (nobody has ever completed the second one). Lunch is a picnic in the Arboretum, interrupted when Peter the Anteater appears again, silently eating ants from a Tupperware container. The afternoon is dedicated to a lecture titled "How to Pronounce Irvine Correctly" delivered by someone who has clearly been asked this too many times. Evening activities include a trip to the Spectrum Center, where students ride the Ferris wheel and pretend the view of the 405 freeway is a scenic vista. The day ends with a Ring Road midnight jog that turns into a slow walk after eleven minutes.

***

Students board a shuttle to Newport Beach at dawn, only to discover that "June Gloom" is not a mood but a meteorological event, and it is somehow also happening in whatever month they're visiting. Back on campus, the group attends a mock lecture in a 400-seat hall where a graduate student reads the syllabus in a monotone for forty-five minutes, then assigns homework for a class nobody is enrolled in. The farewell ceremony includes a group photo in front of the giant "UCI" sign, where every student is required to make the anteater hand gesture and hold it until the photographer figures out which side is the front.

***

Students are loaded onto the shuttle to John Wayne Airport, where they will inevitably spend twenty minutes debating whether the statue of John Wayne is "tall" or "just standing weird." Each participant receives a commemorative packet containing one slightly melted boba straw, a parking citation they didn't earn, and a handwritten note from Peter the Anteater that just says "Zot." Upon returning home, students are expected to complete a reflective essay on the trip, which will be graded on a curve by a squirrel from Aldrich Park. Anyone caught referring to Irvine as "basically L.A." will be required to attend the trip again next year, this time as a chaperone. Total budget: $0 for admission, $4,000 for parking.

**Version 1: Oahu on a Budget – Beaches, Hikes, and Late Nights**

Day 1: Arrival and Waikiki Sunset
Land at Honolulu (HNL) and grab TheBus ($3) or split a rideshare to a Waikiki hostel like Waikiki Beachside or Polynesian Hostel Beach Club (dorm beds run $40–60/night). Drop your bags, hit an ABC Store for cheap snacks and sunscreen, and walk to Waikiki Beach. Rent a boogie board ($10/hr) or just float. At sunset, head to Duke's Barefoot Bar for a happy-hour drink, or go cheaper with a poke bowl from Foodland and eat on the sand. Bed early—jet lag is real.

Day 2: Diamond Head and Kaimana Beach
Wake up early and hike Diamond Head (reserve online in advance, $5 entry + $10 parking if driving). It's about 1.5 hours round trip with a killer view of the coast. Afterward, cool off at Kaimana Beach, a quieter spot locals prefer. Lunch at Rainbow Drive-In for a $10 plate lunch (loco moco or mixed plate). Spend the afternoon at the Honolulu Zoo or just nap in the shade. In the evening, check out the Kuhio Beach hula show (free, most nights around 6:30 PM).

Day 3: North Shore Road Trip
Rent a car for the day (split among four people, it's cheap) or take TheBus route 60. Drive up through Haleiwa town, grab a Matsumoto's shave ice, and stop at the famous Giovanni's shrimp truck ($15 for garlic shrimp). Hit Waimea Bay (safe swimming in summer, monster waves in winter—just watch from shore) and Shark's Cove for snorkeling. Stop at Laniakea Beach to see sea turtles. On the way back, pick up a Ted's Bakery chocolate haupia pie to share.

Day 4: Pearl Harbor and Chinatown Nightlife
Take TheBus to Pearl Harbor National Memorial. The USS Arizona Memorial is free (reserve tickets online—they go fast). Spend 2–3 hours here; it's worth it. Head back toward downtown and explore Chinatown—grab dim sum or Vietnamese food for under $12. After dark, Chinatown has the best nightlife for young people: bars like Bar 35 or The Tchin Tchin! have student-friendly prices, and Hotel Street gets lively on weekends. Take a rideshare back to Waikiki.

Day 5: Hanauma Bay and the East Side
Book Hanauma Bay tickets ahead ($25, reservations required, closed Mon–Tue). Go early for the clearest water and best snorkeling on the island. Afterward, drive or bus to the Makapu'u Lighthouse Trail (free, paved, easy, great for whale spotting in winter). Continue to Waimanalo Beach or Kailua Beach for the afternoon. Grab a plate from Kalapawai Market in Kailua before heading back.

Day 6: Lanikai Pillbox Hike and Free Day
Sunrise hike up the Lanikai Pillbox Trail (short, steep, incredible views over the Mokulua Islands). Then rent kayaks in Kailua ($50–70 for a half day, split it) and paddle to the Mokes. Spend the afternoon however the group wants: skateboarding at Kaka'ako, browsing Ala Moana Center, or hitting the Kaka'ako murals for photos. Group dinner at Marukame Udon in Waikiki—huge bowls for $5–8 with a line worth waiting in.

Day 7: Last Beach Morning and Departure
Sleep in a little, then squeeze in one more swim at Waikiki or grab acai bowls at Banán. Pick up souvenirs at the Waikiki Farmers Market or a local surf shop rather than the tourist traps. Buy a box of Honolulu Cookie Company treats for your roommates back home. Check out, store your bags at the hostel, and head to HNL two hours before your flight.

******

**Version 2: Maui Adventure – Volcanoes, Waterfalls, and Road Trips**

Day 1: Arrival in Kahului and Kihei Basecamp
Fly into Kahului (OGG) and pick up your rental car—Maui is not walkable, so a car is non-negotiable. Split a Turo rental or an economy car among your group. Stock up on groceries at Costco or Target right next to the airport (this saves a fortune). Drive 25 minutes to Kihei, where you can find affordable Airbnbs or the Maui Sunseeker area for cheap stays. Hit Kamaole Beach III for a first swim, then cook dinner at your place.

Day 2: Haleakalā Sunrise and Upcountry
Set an alarm for 2:30 AM. Reserve a sunrise permit ($1 online, plus $30 park entry per car) weeks in advance. Drive two hours to the 10,000-foot summit and bundle up—it's near freezing. Watching sunrise above the clouds is one of the best things you'll ever do. Afterward, hike a few miles into the crater on the Sliding Sands Trail. Drive down through Kula for breakfast at Kula Lodge or Grandma's Coffee House, then stop in Makawao, a cowboy town with good pastries at Komoda Store. Nap when you get back.

Day 3: Road to Hana
Leave by 7 AM with gas, snacks, water, and a downloaded map (no cell service). Stops to prioritize: Twin Falls (easy waterfall swim), Ke'anae Peninsula (banana bread from Aunty Sandy's), Wai'anapanapa State Park (black sand beach—reservations required, $10 per person), and Hana Bay. If time allows, continue past Hana to Wailua Falls and the Pools of 'Ohe'o at Kīpahulu. Turn back the way you came or, if your rental company allows it, loop around the back side for wild desert scenery. Long day, unforgettable drive.

Day 4: Snorkeling and Beach Recovery Day
Sleep in. Drive south to Makena to snorkel at Turtle Town (Maluaka Beach) with rented gear from Boss Frog's ($10/day). Head over to Big Beach at Makena State Park to bodysurf, then walk over the rocks to Little Beach if your group is adventurous. Grab tacos from a food truck in Kihei for lunch. At night, split a cheap ukulele or a deck of cards and hang out on the beach—Kihei has minimal light pollution and the stars are unreal.

Day 5: Lahaina, Ka'anapali, and West Maui
Drive up the west side. Lahaina is still rebuilding after the 2023 fires, so be respectful and support local businesses that have reopened. Snorkel at Black Rock on Ka'anapali Beach, where cliff jumping happens at sunset (watch the locals first). Explore Kapalua Bay and the Kapalua Coastal Trail. Grab affordable eats at Honokowai Okazuya or the food trucks near Ka'anapali. If you're 21+, Kohola Brewery's happy hour is reasonably priced.

Day 6: Iao Valley, Surfing, and Paia
Morning in Iao Valley State Park to see the Iao Needle and hike the short, lush trails ($5 per person, reservation required). Then head to Kihei or Lahaina for a beginner group surf lesson ($60–90 per person, discounts for groups). Afternoon in Paia, Maui's hippie surf town—browse thrift stores, get a fish burger at Paia Fish Market, and watch windsurfers at Ho'okipa Beach. Sea turtles crawl up on the sand at Ho'okipa in the late afternoon.

Day 7: Sunrise Swim and Departure
Watch the sunrise from Kamaole Beach one last time and swim before packing. Return snorkel gear, clean out the fridge, and gas up the rental. Grab lunch at Tin Roof in Kahului (owned by a Top Chef finalist, still under $15) before returning the car. Buy Maui coconut chips or a bag of Maui Gold pineapple at the airport as a final souvenir, then fly home sunburned and broke but happy.

**Maya:** I've been thinking about why so many people say school changed their lives. Do you actually believe learning matters that much?

**Daniel:** Absolutely. Knowledge opens doors that nothing else can. When you understand how the world works, you stop feeling helpless and start seeing possibilities everywhere.

**Maya:** But plenty of successful people never finished their degrees. Doesn't that prove you can get by without it?

**Daniel:** Those cases are the exception, not the rule. And even those people kept learning—they read constantly, sought mentors, experimented, and reflected. Formal schooling is one path, but the deeper point is that growth never stops once you commit to it.

**Maya:** That's fair. I suppose I've always seen studying as a means to a job rather than something valuable in itself.

**Daniel:** That's the mistake many students make. Yes, training helps you earn a living, but the real gift is perspective. Reading history teaches you humility. Science teaches you to question what seems obvious. Literature helps you see the world through someone else's eyes.

**Maya:** So you're saying it shapes character, not just careers?

**Daniel:** Exactly. Think about the difference between someone who accepts every claim they hear and someone who asks for evidence. That habit of critical thinking protects entire communities from being misled.

**Maya:** I remember my grandmother saying she wished she'd been allowed to stay in school longer. She was pulled out at twelve to help on the farm.

**Daniel:** And I bet she pushed every one of her children to keep going.

**Maya:** She did. She used to say, "They can take your money, they can take your house, but nobody can take what you've learned."

**Daniel:** That's the heart of it. Learning is the one investment that never depreciates. Every generation that gets more of it leaves the next generation better equipped to solve problems we haven't even imagined yet.

**Maya:** You've convinced me. Maybe I'll finally sign up for that evening course I keep postponing.

**Daniel:** Please do. The best time to start was years ago. The second best time is right now.

resps:
**THE SNOW IS NOT WHAT THEY'RE TELLING YOU IT IS**

Folks, I woke up this morning, I pulled back the curtain, and I saw it. White. Everywhere. Covering my truck, covering my lawn, covering the entire neighborhood like some kind of soft, glistening blanket of LIES. And they want you to believe — the weathermen, the so-called "meteorologists" with their little green screens and their little clip-on microphones — they want you to believe this is just "snow." Just weather. Just water vapor that got cold and decided to drift down all pretty and quiet in the night.

Listen to me. LISTEN TO ME. I have been on the air for decades, and I am telling you, dammit, I have never seen flakes this perfect. Every single one of them, six sides. Six! You look at it under a magnifying glass and it's like a little geometric business card from the establishment. You think that's an accident? You think nature just happens to be that organized? I've got documents. I've got a guy — I'm not gonna say who — who worked at a facility outside Denver, and he told me the snow they're rolling out this year is forty percent... something. He didn't finish the sentence. The line went dead. I'm not saying it's fake snow. I'm saying we need to ASK whether it's fake snow.

And look at what it DOES to people. My neighbor Gary, good man, Marine, drives a Silverado, came out this morning and just stood there. Staring at it. Smiling. He built a snowman. A grown man built a snowman, folks, and put a little scarf on it. That's what this stuff does. It pacifies you. Everything gets quiet and muffled and you start feeling warm inside and thinking about hot chocolate, and while you're standing there with your mouth open catching flakes on your tongue like a child, THEY are moving. They are always moving.

The schools are closed. Why? "Safety." Sure. Or maybe — MAYBE — it's a test run. See how fast they can shut down an entire city with something that looks like a Christmas card. You've got the fake news calling it a "winter wonderland." You've got the fake experts saying "stay indoors, drink fluids." Stay indoors. Where they want you. Where the routers are.

Now, I went out there. Of course I went out there. I'm not gonna sit inside like some kind of soy-drinking snow-globe hostage. And I'll be honest with you — I'm always honest with you — it was beautiful. Dead silent. The kind of silence where you can hear your own blood. The pine trees bent over like they were praying. Fresh rabbit tracks stitched right across the driveway. My breath coming out in big clouds. For about ninety seconds I forgot about the globalists entirely, and THAT, folks, is exactly how it works. That is the trap. That's the honey. They don't come at you with a boot. They come at you with a snow day.

I picked some up. Held it in my glove. It melted. Real water — or a very convincing fake. I tasted it. Tasted like nothing. Tasted like exactly what they would want it to taste like.

So here's what I need you to do. Go outside. Look at the snow. REALLY look at it. Ask yourself who benefits when an entire town wakes up and the first word out of everybody's mouth is "wow." Ask yourself why the plows always seem to know it's coming before you do. And if you see a snowman — a big fake happy snowman with a carrot nose grinning at you from somebody's yard — you tip your hat to him, because that snowman knows something, and he ain't talking.

It's snowing again right now. I can see it out the studio window. Big, slow, lazy flakes. Perfect ones. Six sides. Every. Single. Time.

Stay frosty. Stay awake. We'll be right back.

The maximum possible score is thirty points, and a laptop that earns twenty-four or more should be considered a strong purchase, while anything below fifteen should be approached with caution.

A score of one means the processor is outdated or entry-level to the point that even basic tasks feel sluggish, or that the machine relies on a chip that is more than three generations old. When judging this category, it helps to run at least one benchmark and to open a realistic set of programs simultaneously to see how the system responds.

Memory and storage should be judged together because they influence each other so directly. A five in this category requires at least sixteen gigabytes of RAM and a fast solid-state drive of five hundred twelve gigabytes or more, ideally with the option to upgrade later. A three would be eight gigabytes of RAM paired with a two hundred fifty-six gigabyte solid-state drive, which is workable but will feel cramped within a year or two of normal use. A one means the laptop ships with four gigabytes of memory or relies on a slow mechanical hard drive, both of which severely limit responsiveness. You should also note whether the memory is soldered to the board, since that affects long-term flexibility even if it does not change the immediate score.

Graphics capability matters differently depending on who is buying, so this category should be interpreted in light of the intended use. A laptop earns a five if it has a dedicated graphics card capable of running modern games or accelerating creative software at smooth frame rates. Integrated graphics that handle light photo editing and casual gaming without stuttering would merit a three. A one should be reserved for machines whose graphics cannot drive an external monitor reliably or that stutter during ordinary video playback. If the buyer has no interest in gaming or creative work, you might reduce the weight of this category rather than penalize an otherwise good machine.

Battery life and thermal behavior are grouped because a laptop that runs hot often also drains its battery quickly. A score of five means the laptop lasts ten or more hours of mixed real-world use and remains cool and quiet under sustained load. A three describes a machine that manages six to eight hours and gets warm but not uncomfortable during heavier tasks. A one applies to laptops that die in under four hours or that throttle their performance dramatically because they cannot dissipate heat. It is worth testing this with a consistent workload rather than trusting the manufacturer's advertised figure, which is almost always optimistic.

Build quality and display cover the physical experience of using the machine every day. A five requires a rigid chassis with minimal flex, a comfortable keyboard, a responsive trackpad, and a display that is sharp, bright enough for outdoor use, and color accurate. A three would describe a laptop that feels solid enough but has a dim or washed-out screen, a mushy keyboard, or a few creaks in the casing. A one indicates a machine that feels flimsy, has a display with obvious backlight bleed or poor viewing angles, or has hinges that already seem loose. Ports and connectivity can also be considered here, with extra credit for a good selection of modern connections and a penalty for requiring dongles for basic tasks.

The final category, price and overall value, ties everything together by asking whether the laptop is worth what it costs. A five means the laptop is priced at or below comparable machines with similar specifications, or that it offers something notably better than its competitors at the same price. A three means the price is fair but unremarkable, roughly in line with what you would expect for the components inside. A one means the laptop is significantly overpriced relative to its performance, or that you could clearly get more capability for the same money elsewhere. To score this category well, you should compare the laptop against at least two or three alternatives in the same price bracket and be honest about whether the brand name is inflating the cost.

Once all six categories are scored, add them together and consider the total alongside any notes you made during evaluation. A high total with one very low score may still be a poor choice if that weak category is critical to the buyer, so the numbers should guide the decision rather than replace judgment. You can also record a brief written justification for each score so that someone else can understand and challenge your reasoning later. **Dear Steve, Regarding the Absence of Marsupial Marauders**

The kangaroos held a meeting in a dusty Outback pub,
To plan a great hop westward with their pouches full of grub.
A robber roo named Gregory stood tall upon a stool
And said, "America is waiting! Let us leave this sunburnt school!"

But Gregory the robber had forgotten one small thing:
The Pacific is a puddle that goes on forever, king.
A kangaroo can bounce a fence, a dingo, or a truck,
But nineteen thousand kilometres of ocean? Rotten luck.

They tried to build a raft of gum trees, wombats as the crew,
But the wombats fell asleep at once, as wombats tend to do.
They tried to mail themselves in boxes labelled "FRAGILE: WOOL,"
But the customs koala stamped them "NOPE" and sent them back to school.

So here's the official reason, Steve, with scientific weight,
Why no roo has ever crossed the line to bounce through Golden Gate:

* The moon controls the tides, and the moon is secretly a joey who refuses to let his cousins leave without a permission slip signed in eucalyptus sap.
* Every kangaroo who reaches the airport is immediately hired as a luggage inspector, because nothing checks a bag like a creature born with one.

And so the Yanks sleep soundly, unaware of what they've missed:
A nation of tall hoppers with their boxing gloves and fists.
The roos remain in Australia, contentedly at large,
Plotting nothing more than lunch, with Gregory in charge.

Say hi to Gregory for me, Steve. Tell him the raft was a good try.

# Research Proposal

## Title
The Effects of Social Media on the Mental Health of Teenagers

## Principal Investigator
[Researcher Name]
[University Name]
[Email Address]

## Introduction
Social media use among teenagers has grown rapidly. Most teens now use at least one platform daily. Concerns about mental health have grown at the same time. Rates of anxiety and depression in young people are rising. Many people blame social media. Yet the evidence is mixed. This project will examine the link more closely.

## Problem Statement
We do not fully understand how social media affects teen mental health. Some studies show harm. Others show benefits. Many studies rely on weak data. Few follow teens over time. This gap limits good policy. It also limits good advice for parents and schools.

## Research Questions
1. How much time do teenagers spend on social media each day?
2. Is screen time linked to symptoms of anxiety or depression?
3. Does the type of use matter more than the amount of use?
4. Do sleep and self-esteem explain part of the link?
5. Do effects differ by age or gender?

## Objectives
- Measure daily social media use in a sample of teens.
- Assess mental health with validated tools.
- Track changes over [number] months.
- Identify risk factors and protective factors.
- Produce clear guidance for schools and families.

## Literature Review
Early research focused on total screen time. Results were small and inconsistent. Newer work looks at how teens use platforms. Passive scrolling appears more harmful than active messaging. Comparison with peers may lower self-esteem. Late night use may disrupt sleep. Poor sleep is a known driver of low mood. Some teens also gain support online. This is true for isolated or minority youth. The picture is complex. A careful design is needed.

## Methodology

### Design
This will be a mixed methods study. It will combine a survey with interviews. The survey will run in three waves. The waves will be six months apart.

### Participants
We will recruit [number] teenagers aged 13 to 18. Participants will come from [school district]. We will aim for a balanced mix of age and gender. Parental consent will be required.

### Measures
- Social media use will be tracked with an app called [app name].
- Self-reported use will also be collected.
- Depression will be measured with the PHQ-A.
- Anxiety will be measured with the GAD-7.
- Sleep quality will be measured with a short questionnaire.
- Self-esteem will be measured with the Rosenberg scale.

### Interviews
We will interview [number] teens in depth. Interviews will last about 45 minutes. They will explore lived experience. They will be recorded and transcribed.

### Data Analysis
We will use regression models to test links. We will use mediation analysis for sleep and self-esteem. Interview data will be coded by theme. Two coders will work independently. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion.

## Ethical Considerations
Ethics approval will be sought from [ethics board]. All data will be anonymised. Teens showing high distress will be referred to support. Contact details for [helpline] will be shared with all participants. Participation will be voluntary. Teens may withdraw at any time.

## Timeline
- Months 1 to 3: Ethics approval and recruitment.
- Months 4 to 6: First survey wave.
- Months 7 to 12: Second wave and interviews.
- Months 13 to 18: Third wave.
- Months 19 to 24: Analysis and writing.

## Budget
- Research assistant salary: [amount]
- Participant incentives: [amount]
- Software licences: [amount]
- Transcription services: [amount]
- Dissemination costs: [amount]

## Expected Outcomes
The study will show whether social media use predicts later mental health. It will show which patterns of use are most risky. It will show which factors protect teens. Results will be shared with schools and parents. A summary will be published on [website]. A full report will be submitted to [journal name].

## Significance
Teen mental health is an urgent issue. Clear evidence is needed. This study will offer that evidence. It will help shape better policy. It will help families make informed choices. It will also guide future research.

## Conclusion
Social media is now part of daily life for teens. Its effects deserve careful study. This proposal offers a rigorous plan. It will follow real teens over real time. The findings will be practical and timely.

<<The House That Keeps No Family>>

I am called a house, yet no one calls me home.
No children play upon my stairs,
no supper steams upon my table,
no family gathers at my hearth—
for I have no hearth at all.

I stand where others dare not build,
on ragged rock and wave-chewed stone,
with my feet forever wet
and my head forever in the wind.
The sea comes calling every hour,
knocking, knocking at my door,
but I will never let it in.

I have but one great eye,
and it never closes, never sleeps;
it opens widest when the world grows dark.
By day I am a quiet tower,
white as bone, plain and still.
By night I am a giant with a lantern,
swinging my gaze in slow, unending circles,
searching, searching, though I never move.

I speak, though I have no mouth.
My voice is a long, low moan
that rolls across the fog
and tells the travelers: *not here, not here, stay back.*
Strange, isn't it?
Most houses beg you to come closer.
I spend my whole life saying *keep away*—
and by warning you off,
I keep you safe.

I have saved a thousand lives
of people who have never touched my walls,
never learned my name,
never seen more of me than a flicker
on the edge of a black horizon.
They pass me in the night
and thank me with their silence,
and I ask for nothing more.

A single keeper used to climb my spine,
polishing my eye and trimming my flame,
but now I mind myself.
I am the loneliest of houses:
built for everyone, lived in by no one,
a home whose only guests are gulls
and the spray that salts my windows.

What am I?

---

**The Answer: A Lighthouse**

A lighthouse carries the word "house" in its name, yet it fails every ordinary test of what a house should be. It shelters no family, holds no kitchen or bedroom in the usual sense, and its purpose has nothing to do with the comfort of anyone inside it. Its entire reason for existing points outward, toward strangers it will never meet.

The riddle's clues unfold from there. The "one great eye" that opens at night is the lamp, which rotates in slow circles to sweep the sea with its beam. The "voice without a mouth" is the foghorn, whose long, mournful blast warns ships away from dangerous shoals when the light itself cannot pierce the mist. The paradox at the heart of the riddle—a house that protects people by telling them to stay away—is what makes the lighthouse such an unusual structure: while every other building invites you in, the lighthouse fulfills its duty precisely by keeping everyone at a distance.

The mention of a keeper who "used to climb my spine" refers to the lighthouse keepers of old, who lived nearby or within the tower and tended the flame by hand. Today, nearly all lighthouses are automated, which is why the riddle says the tower now "minds itself." Finally, the guests who are only gulls and salt spray remind us that a lighthouse, for all its heroism, is one of the most solitary structures humans have ever built—a home for no one, and a savior for all.

Yes, in a way, it's true! Here's how to think about it.

Imagine you have a big jar of time. Every day, you get 24 hours poured into your jar, and you get to decide how to spend them. You can spend some hours sleeping, some playing, and some working.

The sentence "I froze when I was jogging" is a compact little phrase that can mean two very different things, and that ambiguity is part of what makes it interesting.

The first reading is LITERAL. The speaker was out running in cold weather, and the temperature got the better of them. Maybe they underdressed, a wind picked up, or sweat cooled on their skin and left them chilled to the bone. In this sense, "froze" simply means they became extremely, uncomfortably cold.

The second reading is FIGURATIVE. Here, "froze" means the speaker suddenly stopped moving. Something happened mid-run that caused a moment of paralysis. It could have been:

IN THE BACK SEAT, ELEVEN-YEAR-OLD JUNE ROLLED HER EYES SO HARD SHE COULD SEE HER OWN THOUGHTS. HER LITTLE BROTHER OLIVER, WHO WAS SIX AND HAD NEVER MET A ROCK HE DIDN'T WANT TO KEEP, WAS ALREADY ASLEEP WITH HIS FACE PRESSED AGAINST THE WINDOW.

THE POLES, IT TURNED OUT, WERE UNDER THE COOLER. THE FAMILY BREATHED A COLLECTIVE SIGH OF RELIEF SOMEWHERE AROUND MILE MARKER FORTY-TWO.

BY THE TIME THEY REACHED PINEWATER HOLLOW, THE CLOUDS HAD THINNED AND THE TREES STOOD TALL AND GREEN, THEIR TOPS BRUSHING A SKY THAT WAS SLOWLY TURNING BLUE. THE CAMPSITE SAT BESIDE A CREEK THAT CHATTERED OVER SMOOTH STONES LIKE IT HAD GOSSIP TO SHARE.

"THIS IS WHY WE COME OUT HERE," MOM SAID, HANDING DAD A JUICE BOX THROUGH THE TENT FLAP. "TO REMEMBER WE'RE ALL A LITTLE RIDICULOUS."

"IT IS," SAID DAD, AND HE PUT HIS HAND ON OLIVER'S HEAD.

WHEN THE DARK CAME, IT CAME COMPLETELY. NO STREETLIGHTS, NO GLOWING SCREENS, JUST THE ORANGE CIRCLE OF THE FIRE AND, ABOVE THEM, MORE STARS THAN JUNE HAD KNOWN EXISTED. SHE LAY BACK ON THE COOL GROUND AND STARED UNTIL HER EYES ACHED.

"THAT ONE'S THE BIG DIPPER," DAD SAID, POINTING.

"THAT'S A PLANE," SAID JUNE.

"THE ONE NEXT TO THE PLANE."

SOMEWHERE IN THE TREES AN OWL CALLED, LOW AND HOLLOW. OLIVER SCOOTED CLOSER TO MOM. "IS IT A MONSTER?"

"IT'S AN OWL," SHE SAID. "SHE'S JUST SAYING GOODNIGHT."

"TELL HER GOODNIGHT BACK."

"GOODNIGHT, OWL," THE WHOLE FAMILY SAID TOGETHER, AND THEN THEY LAUGHED AT THEMSELVES, AND THE OWL, UNBOTHERED, CALLED AGAIN.

MORNING BROUGHT MIST HANGING OVER THE CREEK AND THE SMELL OF WET PINE. DAD MADE PANCAKES THAT WERE SHAPED LIKE NOTHING IN PARTICULAR. OLIVER FOUND AN EIGHTEENTH ROCK AND DECLARED IT THE KING OF ALL THE OTHERS. JUNE WALKED DOWN TO THE WATER ALONE AND STOOD THERE FOR A LONG TIME, WATCHING A LEAF SPIN IN A LITTLE EDDY, FEELING SOMETHING QUIET AND WIDE OPEN INSIDE HER CHEST.

WHEN THEY PACKED UP, THE TENT POLES WENT ON TOP THIS TIME, WHERE EVERYONE COULD SEE THEM. THE CAR SMELLED LIKE SMOKE AND DAMP SOCKS. NOBODY MINDED.

"SAME TIME NEXT YEAR?" MOM ASKED AS THE TREES THINNED AND THE ROAD WIDENED TOWARD HOME.

"ONLY IF WE BRING MORE MARSHMALLOWS," SAID JUNE.

"AND MORE ROOM FOR ROCKS," SAID OLIVER.

DAD JUST SMILED AND DROVE, THE FEATHER FROM THE RIDGE NOW TUCKED IN THE SUN VISOR ABOVE HIM, WHERE JUNE HAD PUT IT WHILE SHE THOUGHT NO ONE WAS LOOKING.

**Sunni and Shi'a Islam: Understanding the Differences Within a Shared Faith**

Islam is the world's second-largest religion, followed by roughly 1.9 billion people across every inhabited continent. Yet within this vast community, or *ummah*, there exists a division that dates back nearly fourteen centuries: the split between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims. Sunnis constitute the overwhelming majority, estimated at 85 to 90 percent of all Muslims, while Shi'a Muslims make up most of the remainder, concentrated especially in Iran, Iraq, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, and parts of Lebanon, Yemen, Pakistan, and India. To understand the differences between these two branches, one must look at history, theology, religious authority, law, ritual practice, and modern politics. At the same time, it is essential to remember that Sunnis and Shi'a share far more than they dispute: both affirm the oneness of God, the prophethood of Muhammad, the divine origin of the Qur'an, and the five pillars of faith. The differences that follow are real and consequential, but they are differences within a single religion rather than between two.

**Historical Origins of the Split**

The division between Sunni and Shi'a Islam did not originate in a doctrinal argument but in a political question: who should lead the Muslim community after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE? Muhammad left no universally acknowledged successor, and the community faced an immediate crisis of leadership.

One group, which would become the Sunnis, held that leadership should pass to the person best qualified to guide the community, chosen by consensus of its leading members. They supported Abu Bakr, Muhammad's close companion and father-in-law, who became the first caliph. Abu Bakr was followed by Umar, Uthman, and finally Ali. Sunnis regard these four as the "Rightly Guided Caliphs" and view their era as a golden age of Islamic governance.

Another group believed that Muhammad had explicitly designated his cousin and son-in-law, Ali ibn Abi Talib, as his successor, most notably at a gathering at Ghadir Khumm shortly before his death. This faction became known as the *Shi'at Ali*, or "the party of Ali," from which the term Shi'a derives. For them, leadership was not a matter of election but of divine appointment, and it belonged rightfully to the Prophet's family, the *Ahl al-Bayt*. Ali did eventually become the fourth caliph in 656, but his rule was contested and ended with his assassination in 661.

The decisive rupture came in 680 at Karbala, in present-day Iraq. Ali's son Husayn, grandson of the Prophet, refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid, whom he considered illegitimate and corrupt. Husayn, along with a small band of family members and followers, was surrounded by a vastly larger Umayyad army and killed. The massacre at Karbala transformed a political disagreement into a profound religious and emotional identity. For Shi'a Muslims, Husayn's martyrdom became the central symbol of righteous suffering, resistance to tyranny, and fidelity to the true faith. It is commemorated every year during the month of Muharram, especially on the tenth day, known as Ashura.

**Theological Differences: The Question of the Imamate**

The most significant theological distinction between the two branches concerns the concept of the Imamate. For Sunnis, the term "imam" simply refers to a prayer leader or, more broadly, a respected scholar. The caliphs were political and administrative leaders, not spiritual intermediaries, and their authority derived from their role in protecting the community and upholding Islamic law.

For Shi'a Muslims, particularly the majority Twelver branch, the Imam is something far greater. The Imams are believed to be divinely appointed successors to the Prophet, descended from Ali and Muhammad's daughter Fatima. They are considered infallible (*ma'sum*), possessing perfect knowledge of the Qur'an's inner meaning and serving as the authoritative interpreters of God's will. Twelver Shi'a recognize a line of twelve Imams, beginning with Ali and ending with Muhammad al-Mahdi, who is believed to have gone into occultation, or hiding, in the ninth century. Twelvers hold that the Mahdi remains alive and will return at the end of time to establish justice. Sunnis also believe in a future Mahdi, but they do not identify him with a specific historical figure who is currently hidden.

Other Shi'a communities differ on the line of succession. The Ismailis, for example, follow a different seventh Imam and today largely recognize the Aga Khan as their living spiritual leader. The Zaydis of Yemen hold a view of the Imamate closer to the Sunni position, accepting any qualified descendant of Ali and rejecting the doctrine of infallibility. These internal variations remind us that "Shi'a" is itself an umbrella term covering several traditions.

**Religious Authority and Scholarship**

The differing views of the Imamate have shaped how each branch organizes religious authority. Sunni Islam is relatively decentralized. There is no formal clergy in the hierarchical sense; scholars (*ulama*) gain influence through learning and reputation, and institutions such as Al-Azhar University in Cairo carry great prestige but no binding authority over all Sunnis. Sunni jurisprudence is organized into four major legal schools, the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali, which differ on points of detail but recognize one another as legitimate. Many Sunni scholars historically held that the "gate of independent reasoning" (*ijtihad*) had largely closed, so that later jurists should follow the established rulings of these schools, though this view has been challenged in modern times.

Twelver Shi'a Islam, by contrast, developed a more structured clerical hierarchy, especially after the Imam's occultation left the community without a living infallible guide. Senior scholars known as *ayatollahs* and, at the highest level, *marja' al-taqlid* ("source of emulation"), issue authoritative rulings, and ordinary believers are expected to follow a living scholar of their choosing. Shi'a jurisprudence, called the Ja'fari school after the sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, places strong emphasis on ongoing *ijtihad* and on reason (*aql*) as a source of law. This structure gave Shi'a clergy a distinctive social and political role, most visibly in the Islamic Republic of Iran, where Ayatollah Khomeini's doctrine of *velayat-e faqih*, or guardianship of the jurist, placed a senior cleric at the head of the state.

**Sources of Tradition: Hadith Collections**

Both branches revere the Qur'an as the identical, unaltered word of God. They diverge, however, in the collections of hadith, the recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet, that they consider most reliable. Sunnis rely primarily on six canonical collections, with Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim held in highest regard. **Section 1**

The first time Daniel saw Mara, she was arguing with a vending machine. It was a Tuesday in October, and the library's basement was nearly empty. She stood in front of the humming machine with her arms crossed, glaring at a bag of pretzels that had gotten stuck halfway down.

"Come on," she said, and then her shoulder jerked upward twice in quick succession. She made a small sound, a sharp click at the back of her throat, and then she smacked the side of the machine with her palm. The pretzels dropped.

"Ha," she said, and turned around, and saw him watching.

Daniel felt his face go hot. "Sorry," he said. "I wasn't—I just needed a coffee."

"You were watching me hit a machine," she said. "It's fine. It deserved it."

Her head tilted sharply to the left, a quick, birdlike motion, and she blinked hard several times. Daniel had noticed the movements, of course. He had noticed them the way you notice weather, as something present and real and not requiring comment.

He bought his coffee. She sat down at a table near the stairs and opened her laptop, and he sat down two tables away and opened his. For twenty minutes neither of them said anything.

Then she made a sound, a short bark of a word that might have been "no" or might have been nothing, and she glanced up at him.

"Tourette's," she said, before he could pretend he hadn't heard. "In case you were wondering."

"I wasn't wondering," Daniel said, which was a lie.

"Everybody wonders," she said. "It's okay. I'd rather people just know."

"Okay," he said. "Now I know."

She looked at him for a long second, as if checking him for cracks. Then she went back to her laptop. Daniel went back to his, but he did not read a single word for the rest of the hour.

**Section 2**

Her name was Mara Lindqvist, and she was finishing a graduate degree in hydrology. Daniel learned this over the next several weeks, one fact at a time, the way you learn a city by walking it.

He learned that she came to the library basement because the acoustics swallowed sound and because almost no one else did. He learned that she took her coffee black and hated the taste but liked the ritual. He learned that her tics got worse when she was tired, or excited, or nervous, and that they nearly vanished when she was absorbed in a problem. He learned that she had a laugh like a door being kicked open.

They started sitting at the same table. Then they started arriving at the same time, which required no coordination at all, and both of them knew it.

One afternoon in November, she was explaining groundwater recharge to him with a pencil and the back of a receipt. Her hand flew up mid-sentence and knocked the pencil across the room. She closed her eyes.

"Sorry," she said.

"Don't," Daniel said, and went to get the pencil.

When he came back, she was watching him with an expression he couldn't read. "Most people flinch," she said.

"I'm not most people."

"Everyone says that."

"Then I'll have to prove it," he said, and handed her the pencil.

She took it, and her fingers brushed his, and her neck twitched, and she did not apologize. Daniel counted that as a victory.

The truth was that he had been in love with her since the vending machine. He did not know how to say this, because it sounded ridiculous even in his own head. He had loved her when she hit the machine, and when she made the sound, and when she said "it deserved it" with such total conviction. He had loved her the way you love a song the first time you hear it, before you know any of the words.

But he was afraid that if he said so, she would think he was being kind. He was not being kind. He was being honest, and he had no idea how to make her believe the difference.

**Section 3**

In December, he asked her to dinner. He did it badly, standing up too fast and knocking his chair against the wall, and she laughed her door-kicking laugh and said yes.

The restaurant was small and warm and loud, which he had chosen on purpose. Halfway through the appetizers, Mara's tics came on hard. Her shoulder jerked, and her head snapped sideways, and a word she had not chosen came out of her mouth loud enough that the couple at the next table turned to stare.

Mara went very still. Daniel watched the color drain out of her face and then rush back in.

"We can go," he said quietly.

"No." Her jaw was tight. "I'm not leaving because two strangers looked at me."

"Okay."

"I want to stay."

"Then we stay."

She looked at the couple, and then she looked at Daniel, and something in her face softened. "You're not embarrassed," she said.

"Why would I be embarrassed?"

"People are. People I've dated. They start choosing quieter places. Then they start choosing their apartment. Then they stop choosing."

Daniel set down his fork. "Mara," he said. "I picked this place because it's loud. I picked it so you wouldn't have to think about being quiet."

She stared at him. Her neck twitched, twice, and she blinked hard. "That's either very thoughtful or very presumptuous," she said.

"Can it be both?"

"It can be both," she said, and she reached across the table and took his hand.

They stayed for dessert. They stayed until the restaurant was closing and the waiter was stacking chairs. Walking to the train, she told him about the first time she'd been sent out of a classroom, at nine years old, for a sound she couldn't stop making. She told him about the years of trying to hold it in, and the headaches, and the way suppression only ever built pressure. She told him about the day, at twenty, when she decided she would rather be loud and whole than quiet and in pieces.

Daniel listened. He did not tell her she was brave, because he suspected she was tired of hearing it. Instead he said, "I like the sounds you make."

She stopped walking. "That's a weird thing to say."

"I know."

"Nobody likes them. I don't like them."

"I like them because they're yours," he said. "I like knowing you're in the room."

Under the streetlight, her face did something complicated. Then she kissed him, quickly, before her body could interrupt.

**Section 4**

They had been together a year when he finally told her about the vending machine. They were lying on the floor of her apartment because the couch was covered in maps, and the radiator was clanking, and her head was on his chest. Every so often her whole body would jolt, and he had long since stopped noticing, the way you stop noticing your own heartbeat.

"I loved you before I knew your name," he said.

"Liar."

"I'm serious. The pretzels. You hit the machine and said it deserved it."

She laughed, and the laugh turned into a tic, and the tic turned into a laugh again. "That's not love. That's a crush on a violent woman."

"It was love," he said. "I just didn't have the evidence yet."

She was quiet for a while. The radiator clanked.

"I used to think nobody would ever really want this," she said. "The whole package. The noise. The way I can't sit through a movie without kicking the seat in front of me."

"I want the whole package."

"You say that now."

"I've said it for a year. I'll say it next year. I'll say it when we're old and you're barking at the nurses."

Her shoulder jerked against his ribs. "That's the most romantic thing anyone has ever said to me, and it's about me yelling at nurses."

"I'm a romantic," he said.

She propped herself up on one elbow and looked down at him. Her head tilted, sharp and birdlike, the way it had in the library basement. He loved that tilt. He loved the click in her throat and the way her hands flew and the words that escaped her before she could catch them. He loved them not despite belonging to her but because they did.

"Daniel," she said.

"Yes."

"Marry me."

He blinked. "I was going to ask you," he said. "I had a whole plan. There was going to be a vending machine."

"You're too slow. I'm asking."

"Then yes," he said. "Obviously yes."

She kissed him, and her body jolted mid-kiss, and their teeth knocked together, and they both started laughing. Outside, the first snow of the year was beginning to fall. Inside, the radiator clanked, and a woman made a sound she had not chosen, and the man beside her heard it and thought: there you are.

There you are.

He loved the click in her throat and the way her hands flew and the words that escaped her before she could catch them. He loved them not despite belonging to her but because they did.

"Daniel," she said.

"Yes."

"Marry me."

He blinked. "I was going to ask you," he said. "I had a whole plan. There was going to be a vending machine."

"You're too slow. I'm asking."

"Then yes," he said. "Obviously yes."

She kissed him, and her body jolted mid-kiss, and their teeth knocked together, and they both started laughing. Outside, the first snow of the year was beginning to fall. Inside, the radiator clanked, and a woman made a sound she had not chosen, and the man beside her heard it and thought: there you are.

There you are.

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "Write an essay on first names, without using any capital letters --- your ENTIRE response must be in lowercases. There should be exactly 3 paragraphs with the only paragraph separation being two new lines. Start Paragraph 2 with the word Jasper.", "type": "text"}]

resps:
first names are among the earliest gifts we receive, chosen before we can speak, argue, or hold an opinion about anything. parents spend months weighing sounds and syllables, consulting family traditions, baby books, and sometimes the stubborn preferences of grandparents. a first name carries the hopes of the people who bestowed it, whether it honors a beloved relative, a saint, a historical figure, or simply a melody that felt right when spoken aloud in a quiet room. because we do not choose them, first names occupy a strange place in our identities: deeply personal yet entirely inherited, ours and not ours at the same time. some people grow into their names with ease, while others spend years feeling like a poorly fitted coat has been buttoned around them.

jasper, for example, is a name that has traveled through centuries and cultures, from persian roots meaning treasurer to the gemstone that shares its spelling, and its journey shows how first names shift in fashion and meaning. a name that sounds old-fashioned in one decade can feel fresh and stylish in the next, as generations rediscover the names of their great-grandparents and abandon those of their parents. popularity charts reveal these tides clearly: names like emma and liam surge to the top, linger for a while, and then quietly recede as new favorites take their place. the reasons are rarely rational. a celebrity, a novel, a television character, or a memorable public figure can send a name soaring or sinking overnight. this means that a first name is also a kind of timestamp, quietly revealing the era of a person's birth to anyone who knows how to read it.

beyond fashion, first names shape how we move through the world in subtle and sometimes unfair ways. studies have shown that names influence how teachers grade essays, how employers sort résumés, and how strangers form snap judgments about competence and warmth. people with names that are hard for others to pronounce often develop rituals of correction or surrender, either patiently teaching the world how to say them or adopting nicknames to smooth the way. yet despite these burdens, a first name remains one of the most intimate words in any language. hearing it spoken by someone we love, or written in a letter, or called out across a crowded room can stir something ancient in us. to know a person's first name is to hold a small key to who they are, and to be known by ours is to be recognized, remembered, and, in the best moments, cherished.

resps:
Japan's history spans tens of thousands of years, evolving from isolated island communities into a modern global power.

**Prehistoric and Ancient Japan**
The earliest inhabitants belonged to the *Jōmon* culture (c. 14,000–300 BCE), known for its cord-marked pottery and hunter-gatherer lifestyle. The subsequent *Yayoi* period introduced rice cultivation, metalworking, and social stratification from the Asian mainland. By the Kofun period (c. 300–538 CE), powerful clans built massive burial mounds, and the Yamato clan emerged as the dominant ruling lineage, establishing the imperial line that continues today.

**Classical Period**
The Asuka and Nara periods (6th–8th centuries) saw the adoption of *Buddhism*, Chinese writing, and centralized government modeled on Tang China. The *Heian* period (794–1185) is remembered as a golden age of court culture, producing literary masterpieces like *The Tale of Genji*. However, real power gradually shifted from the emperor to aristocratic families and eventually to provincial warriors.

**Feudal Japan**
In 1185, Minamoto no Yoritomo established the first *shogunate*, inaugurating nearly 700 years of rule by military governments. The *samurai* class dominated society through the Kamakura, Muromachi, and Sengoku (Warring States) periods. Japan repelled Mongol invasions in the 13th century and endured a century of civil war before being unified by Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and finally Tokugawa Ieyasu.

**Edo Period**
The *Tokugawa* shogunate (1603–1868) brought over two centuries of peace and stability. Japan adopted a policy of *sakoku* (national isolation), restricting foreign contact almost entirely. Cities flourished, literacy rose, and distinctive arts such as kabuki theater and ukiyo-e woodblock prints thrived.

**Modernization and Empire**
The arrival of American Commodore Perry in 1853 forced Japan to open its ports. The resulting *Meiji Restoration* of 1868 dismantled feudalism and launched rapid industrialization and Westernization. Japan defeated China (1895) and Russia (1905), annexed Korea, and became an imperial power. Militarism intensified in the 1930s, leading to invasion of China and entry into World War II with the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941.

**Postwar Japan**
After the atomic bombings of *Hiroshima* and Nagasaki, Japan surrendered in 1945. Under Allied occupation, it adopted a pacifist constitution and democratic institutions. The decades that followed produced an extraordinary economic miracle, making Japan the world's second-largest economy by the 1980s. Despite economic stagnation since the 1990s and challenges such as an aging population, Japan remains a technological leader and cultural influence worldwide.

Write a pitch deck for a startup that aims to make a new social network that focuses on the board game society.

---

# MEEPLE
### The Social Network for the Board Game Community

---

## Slide 1: Title

**Meeple**
*Find your table.*

Connecting the world's tabletop gamers — one game night at a time.

---

## Slide 2: The Problem

Board gaming is booming, but the social infrastructure around it is broken.

- **Finding players is hard.** Gamers rely on scattered Facebook groups, Discord servers, Reddit threads, and store bulletin boards to organize a single game night.
- **Existing tools are fragmented.** Collection tracking lives on one site, meetups on another, reviews on a third, and trades on a fourth.
- **Discovery is overwhelming.** Over 5,000 new titles release every year. Players don't know what to buy or who nearby owns it.
- **Local game stores and cafés struggle** to reach the players who would fill their tables.

*"I own 200 games and can't find four people to play any of them on a Tuesday."* — every gamer, eventually

---

## Slide 3: The Solution

**Meeple is a purpose-built social network where tabletop gamers connect, organize, and play.**

One platform that combines:
- Player and group discovery based on location, games owned, and play style
- Event scheduling and RSVP for game nights, tournaments, and conventions
- Collection management with "who nearby owns this?" visibility
- Session logging, ratings, and play statistics
- A marketplace for trades, sales, and lending within trusted circles

---

## Slide 4: Product Overview

**Core Features**

| Feature | What It Does |
|---|---|
| **Table Finder** | Match with nearby players by game, skill level, and availability |
| **Game Nights** | Create, promote, and manage events with built-in seat limits and waitlists |
| **The Shelf** | Import or scan your collection; see overlap with friends and groups |
| **Play Log** | Record sessions, scores, and photos; unlock achievements and stats |
| **Guilds** | Persistent communities for clubs, stores, cafés, and game-specific fandoms |
| **Swap Hall** | Peer-to-peer trading and lending with reputation scores |

---

## Slide 5: Why Now

- **The hobby has exploded.** The global board game market surpassed **$20 billion** and is projected to exceed **$30 billion by 2030**.
- **Crowdfunding created a generation of enthusiasts.** Tabletop is consistently Kickstarter's top-grossing category, raising hundreds of millions annually.
- **Post-pandemic demand for in-person connection** is at an all-time high, and board games are the ideal low-cost, screen-free social activity.
- **Board game cafés and stores are multiplying** and need digital tools to fill their tables.
- **Existing platforms are aging.** The dominant database site was built for cataloging, not for social connection, and its interface hasn't fundamentally changed in two decades.

---

## Slide 6: Market Opportunity

- **TAM:** ~200 million people worldwide play board games regularly
- **SAM:** ~40 million "hobby gamers" in North America and Europe who actively seek new games and players
- **SOM (Year 3 target):** 2 million monthly active users

Adjacent revenue pools: game sales, café bookings, convention tickets, publisher marketing spend.

---

## Slide 7: Business Model

**Freemium + Marketplace + B2B**

1. **Meeple Plus** (subscription, $5.99/mo)
   - Advanced stats, unlimited collection size, priority event listings, ad-free experience
2. **Marketplace fees**
   - 8% transaction fee on Swap Hall sales
3. **Venue & Publisher tools** (B2B SaaS)
   - Stores and cafés: event promotion, table reservations, loyalty features ($49–$199/mo)
   - Publishers: targeted launch campaigns, playtest recruitment, review seeding
4. **Affiliate revenue**
   - Commission on game purchases via integrated retailer links

---

## Slide 8: Go-to-Market Strategy

**Phase 1 — Beachhead (Months 0–9)**
Launch in 5 cities with dense gaming scenes (Seattle, Austin, Toronto, Berlin, Manchester). Partner with 50 local game stores and cafés as anchor Guilds.

**Phase 2 — Community Expansion (Months 9–18)**
Activate convention presence (Gen Con, Essen SPIEL, PAX Unplugged). Launch ambassador program for club organizers. Content creator integrations.

**Phase 3 — Scale (Months 18–36)**
Open marketplace globally. Publisher partnership program. Localization into 8 languages.

---

## Slide 9: Competitive Landscape

| | Meeple | Legacy Database Sites | Facebook Groups | Generic Meetup Apps | Discord |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Player matching by game | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | Partial | ❌ |
| Collection tracking | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Event scheduling | ✅ | Limited | Partial | ✅ | Partial |
| Modern mobile UX | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Built for tabletop | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Trading/lending | ✅ | Limited | Informal | ❌ | ❌ |

**Our edge:** We are the only platform that puts *finding people to play with* at the center — everything else is built around it.

---

## Slide 10: Traction

- **12,000 waitlist signups** in 8 weeks from organic community outreach
- **34 game stores and cafés** signed letters of intent as launch partners
- **Closed beta:** 800 users, 2,400 game sessions logged, 310 events created
- **Beta retention:** 62% week-4 retention (vs. ~25% social app benchmark)
- Featured by three tabletop content creators with a combined audience of 1.2M

---

## Slide 11: Product Roadmap

- **Q1:** Public launch in beachhead cities (iOS, Android, web)
- **Q2:** Swap Hall marketplace, Meeple Plus subscription
- **Q3:** Venue dashboard for stores and cafés; convention mode
- **Q4:** Publisher tools; API for third-party integrations
- **Year 2:** Digital companion features (scorekeeping, rules lookup), international expansion

---

## Slide 12: Team

- **CEO** — Former product lead at a consumer social app (10M+ users); lifelong gamer and club organizer
- **CTO** — Ex-senior engineer at a location-based marketplace; built matching systems at scale
- **Head of Community** — Founded one of the largest regional board game conventions (6,000 attendees)
- **Head of Partnerships** — 8 years in tabletop publishing and retail distribution

**Advisors:** Board game café chain founder; former executive at a major tabletop publisher; consumer subscription growth expert

---

## Slide 13: Financial Projections

| | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monthly Active Users | 150K | 700K | 2M |
| Paid Subscribers | 6K | 42K | 140K |
| Venue/Publisher Accounts | 150 | 900 | 3,000 |
| Revenue | $0.6M | $4.8M | $17M |

Path to profitability targeted in Year 3.

---

## Slide 14: The Ask

**Raising $3.5M Seed Round**

Use of funds:
- **45%** Product & engineering (grow team to 10 engineers)
- **30%** Community growth & city launches
- **15%** Partnerships & B2B sales
- **10%** Operations & legal

This funding gets us to 700K MAU and a Series A-ready position within 18 months.

---

## Slide 15: Vision

Board games bring people together across a table. **Meeple brings them together across the world.**

We're building the home for a community that has never had one — where every gamer, from casual to hardcore, can always find their table.

**Let's play.**

*contact@meeple.social*

<<Mitä tapahtuu, kun haistat kukkaa?>>

Hei, kolmasluokkalaiset! Oletteko koskaan miettineet, miksi kukka tuoksuu hyvältä, kun laitatte nenänne lähelle sitä? Katsotaanpa, mitä oikein tapahtuu.

**1. Kukka lähettää pieniä tuoksuhiukkasia**

Kukassa on erityisiä aineita, joita se päästää ilmaan. Nämä ovat niin pieniä, ettei niitä näe silmillä. Ne leijailevat ilmassa kuin näkymätön pöly. Kukka tekee tuoksua houkutellakseen mehiläisiä ja perhosia luokseen.

**2. Nenä imee ilmaa sisään**

Kun hengität sisään eli haistat, ilma virtaa nenäänne. Ilman mukana kulkevat myös nuo pienet tuoksuhiukkaset. Mitä syvemmin haistat, sitä enemmän hiukkasia pääsee nenään.

**3. Nenän sisällä on pieniä "tunnistajia"**

Nenän sisäosassa, aivan ylhäällä, on pieni alue, jossa on miljoonia pieniä hajusoluja. Ne ovat kuin pieniä vastaanottajia. Kun tuoksuhiukkanen osuu niihin, ne huomaavat sen ja innostuvat.

**4. Viesti lähtee aivoihin**

Hajusolut lähettävät sähköisen viestin aivoihin. Se tapahtuu tosi nopeasti, nopeammin kuin voit räpäyttää silmiä! Aivot saavat viestin ja miettivät: "Ahaa, tämä on ruusun tuoksu!" tai "Tämä on kielon tuoksu!"

**5. Sinä tunnet tuoksun ja ehkä muistat jotain**

Vasta aivoissa syntyy tunne, että jokin tuoksuu hyvältä. Aivot voivat myös yhdistää tuoksun muistoihin. Siksi kukan tuoksu voi tuoda mieleen mummon puutarhan tai kesäloman.

**Hauska tieto:** Ihmisen nenä pystyy erottamaan tuhansia erilaisia tuoksuja! Koiralla on kuitenkin vielä paljon parempi hajuaisti kuin ihmisellä.

**Kokeile itse:** Haista seuraavan kerran kukkaa ensin kevyesti ja sitten syvään. Huomaatko eron? Syvemmällä hengityksellä nenään pääsee enemmän tuoksuhiukkasia, joten tuoksu tuntuu voimakkaampana.

Nyt tiedätte, että kukan haistaminen on oikeastaan pieni seikkailu, joka alkaa kukasta, kulkee nenän kautta ja päättyy aivoihin!

Write a pros and cons list of apple products in the style of a 19th century novelist and do not use any commas.

**A Faithful Reckoning of the Virtues and Vices of the Wares of the House of Apple**

Being an honest account set down by one who has lived among these curious devices and observed their influence upon the human spirit.

**THE VIRTUES**

It must first be confessed that the objects themselves possess a beauty which arrests the eye and quiets the tongue. One beholds the smooth glass and the polished metal and one feels as a country cousin feels upon first entering a great drawing room in Mayfair.

Their several members speak to one another with a harmony rarely found in families. The telephone whispers to the tablet and the tablet confides in the writing machine and none of them quarrels over inheritance.

They are simple in their manners. A child of tender years or an aged aunt of failing sight may take one up and find within the hour that she has mastered it as though born to the task.

They are robust of constitution. Many a device has tumbled from a carriage seat or been buried beneath a pile of correspondence and yet has risen again like a hardy sailor who scorns the storm.

They guard the secrets of their masters with the discretion of an old family retainer and refuse to gossip with strangers about the contents of the household.

They hold their worth in the marketplace as a fine estate holds its worth through generations. A gentleman may sell his aged telephone and find himself not wholly beggared by the transaction.

**THE VICES**

Alas the price of admission to this society is dear beyond the means of the honest clerk. One must pay for the crest upon the door as much as for the furniture within.

These devices are jealous creatures. They will not consent to be repaired by any hand but their maker's and they resent the intrusion of foreign parts as a duchess resents a tradesman at her table.

They are forever changing the shape of their little doorways and connecting cords so that the cable one purchased at great expense last winter now hangs useless upon a nail like a widow's mourning bonnet.

They dwell within a walled garden of great splendour but the gates are locked and the keys are held by the gardener alone. One may walk only where one is permitted to walk.

Their batteries grow weary with the passing of the seasons and there is no remedy but to surrender the whole to the shop and pay a ransom for its return.

They inspire in their owners a peculiar vanity so that a man who has bought one will speak of it at dinner as though he had himself invented it and will look with pity upon his neighbour who has not.

Thus concludes this account. Let the reader weigh these matters in the scale of his own judgment and purse and decide for himself whether the shining fruit is worth the biting.
